sources.news_title: Trump calls off Iran strikes, demands Strait of Hormuz reopened
sources.text:
President Donald Trump said on Saturday he agreed to cancel an attack on Iran so the countries could "rapidly make a deal" that includes the "complete and total opening" of the Strait of Hormuz.
"The U.S.A. is locked and loaded and ready to go against the Islamic Republic of Iran, at levels of Military Terror, Strength, and Power not seen since World War II," Trump said in a post on Truth Social on Saturday night.
"Despite this, we have just been asked by Iran, and other Middle Eastern Countries, to hold off any attack in that the perimeters of a deal has been agreed to," he said, adding later that he had agreed "for the benefit of the world."
It comes after Saudi Arabia’s Prince Mohammed bin Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud called Trump to urge de-escalation and diplomacy, Saudi Arabia’s official state news agency reported on Sunday.
The White House previously said that Trump was weighing new strikes on Iran while the U.S. government has urged Americans in the Middle East to have heightened vigilance, and be prepared for flight cancellations and travel disruption.
America and Iran have exchanged strikes and counter-strikes since their ceasefire broke down in June.
Trump’s Conditional Reprieve for Iran
Trump’s announcement came one day after CBS News reported that the United States and Israel were preparing a major bombing campaign against Iranian energy infrastructure, potentially beginning over the weekend.
The proposed targets included power plants and oil refineries, while senior officials also discussed cutting electricity across Tehran. Trump had not issued a final order, according to the outlet, which cited sources briefed on the talks.
Axios separately reported, citing a U.S. official, that Trump was seriously considering strikes within days as a means of pressuring Tehran to accept U.S. terms in ceasefire negotiations. The possible operation could have brought Israel back into direct combat against Iran and risked renewed Iranian missile attacks on Israel.
Trump’s decision to cancel the attack is conditional, however, as he said it is "subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL." He added that Israel had joined the U.S. commitment.
The comments also came as Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian weighed in on X Sunday, writing, "The memorandum that was signed is the result of the collective wisdom of Shura Council's members, and all members are in sympathy with it. I believe this memorandum will be the center of gravity of our foreign relations in the future."
He added: "We must strive to compel the enemy to remain committed to what it has signed. The security of the country, the region, and our allies will be enhanced by this memorandum."
Former National Counterterrorism Center Director Joe Kent, who resigned earlier this year over the administration's Iran policy, also welcomed Trump's decision.
In a post on X Sunday, he called the move "a good decision" and argued that using military force to reopen the Strait of Hormuz risked "a catastrophic escalation into a bloody, years-long war." Kent urged Trump to withdraw U.S. troops from the region and pursue reopening the waterway through diplomacy and sanctions relief rather than force.
Before Trump’s announcement, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman spoke with the president and emphasized "the need to prioritize dialogue to reduce escalation," according to the Saudi Press Agency. He also called for efforts to secure calm, enable diplomatic solutions and prevent the conflict from widening.
Why Saudi Arabia Fears Further Escalation With Iran
Saudi Arabia has reason to fear that renewed U.S. strikes on Iran could expose the kingdom to retaliation from Tehran and its allied groups across the region.
The country faces potential threats on several fronts. Iranian attacks on infrastructure and vessels in the Persian Gulf have disrupted operations along Saudi Arabia’s eastern coast, while Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi movement has targeted shipping in the Red Sea—the alternative route for Saudi energy exports. The Houthis also control territory along the kingdom’s southern border and have previously launched cross-border missile attacks.
To the north, Iran-aligned militias in Iraq have targeted Saudi energy infrastructure with drones. U.S. and Saudi fighter aircraft responded on July 28 by striking weapons and logistics sites in eastern Iraq following more than 30 drone attacks over 72 hours, according to U.S. Central Command.
The threat to energy infrastructure is particularly sensitive for Riyadh. Saudi Arabia remains one of the world’s largest oil exporters, and attacks on production facilities, ports or shipping routes could disrupt international supplies and damage the kingdom’s economy. Escalation in both the Persian Gulf and Red Sea could also restrict its options for moving oil to overseas markets.
A widening conflict could also undermine Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s Vision 2030 program, which seeks to reduce Saudi Arabia’s reliance on oil and establish the kingdom as a global center for investment, logistics and tourism. Prolonged instability threatens investor confidence, supply chains and the development projects at the heart of that transformation.
Saudi Arabia has responded by strengthening its defenses without abandoning diplomacy. Riyadh has established a 14-country maritime defense alliance to protect shipping and freedom of navigation through strategic waterways.

sources.news_title: Trump Says He Called Off Impending Attack On Iran, Insists Deal Is Close
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump said he has decided to "hold off" on any new attacks on Iran, saying "the perimeters" of a deal have been agreed to with Tehran and adding that Israel was joining him in the commitment.
"The U.S.A. is locked and loaded and ready to go against the Islamic Republic of Iran, at levels of Military Terror, Strength, and Power not seen since World War II. Despite this, we have just been asked by Iran, and other Middle Eastern Countries, to hold off any attack in that the perimeters of a deal has been agreed to," Trump posted on Truth Social late on August 1.
"This would include the Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT, and an end to Iran's nuclear threat."
"Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL," he wrote, adding that Israel joins him in this "commitment."
However, according to Iranian media, military sources in Iran denied Trump's claim that Tehran had asked Washington to refrain from launching new attacks.
Iran’s Mehr News Agency on August 2 quoted the unnamed sources as saying Trump's statement was "simply a new lie" and an attempt to "blackmail the rulers of the Persian Gulf and pressure them with threats."
The sources claimed that Iranian forces were at the highest level of readiness and prepared for any eventuality.
Trump has often threatened major attacks on Iran only to call them off, claiming an agreement between Washington and Tehran was imminent. Until now, a lasting peace agreement has been elusive, with tit-for-tat strikes by both sides resuming.
Although Trump initially said the elimination of Tehran's nuclear threat was the major aim of the US-Israeli war with Iran, which began on February 28, in recent weeks he has focused on the free flow of traffic through the important Strait of Hormuz.
More than 20 percent of the world's oil and gas supplies moved through the strait prewar, but Iran has at times effectively shut down the waterway, including with attacks on ships it said had not received proper approval from Tehran. Iran has also threatened to impose fees or tolls on ships in the strait.
The United States and other countries have insisted the strait is an international waterway and is not under the control of any nation.
Washington and Tehran signed a 60-day memorandum of understanding (MOU) on June 17 aimed at ending hostilities and reopening the strait. However, disputes over the meaning of the terms in the agreement have led to fresh attacks by both sides.
Trump told Axios on July 23 that he was seriously considering "a massive attack" on Iran. But he later backed down from the threat, saying on July 27 that a new round of diplomacy with Iran could produce a breakthrough, although he has always kept open the possibility of further strikes.
Israel, which is conducting a separate war with Hezbollah militants in Lebanon, has often resisted peace deals suggested by the US administration, saying it would continue its attacks as long as necessary.
Iran-backed Hezbollah, a militant group and political party that controls much of southern Lebanon, is considered a terrorist organization by the US, while the European Union has blacklisted its armed wing but not its political branch.

US PRESIDENT DONALD Trump claimed Middle East allies have reached the parameters of a deal to end the Iran war and said that he would hold off on ordering new strikes in the five-month-old conflict.
In a social media post on Sunday morning, Trump added that the emerging deal “would include the Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT, and an end to Iran’s nuclear threat.”
“The U.S.A. is locked and loaded and ready to go against the Islamic Republic of Iran, at levels of Military Terror, Strength, and Power not seen since World War II,” he said.
“Despite this, we have just been asked by Iran, and other Middle Eastern Countries, to hold off any attack in that the perimeters of a deal has been agreed to.
“Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL.”
He added that Israel has agreed to join the US in the commitment to try to complete the agreement with Iran that would bring about an end to the war.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the kingdom’s de facto leader, raised concerns about the US potentially escalating the conflict with Iran during a phone call with Trump on Saturday, a person familiar with the leaders’ discussion told the Associated Press.
The Saudis, according to the person briefed on the substance of the call, are concerned that if the US targets Iran’s energy infrastructure or carries out massive strikes on other key infrastructure that Tehran could respond by carrying out attacks on the kingdom’s and other Gulf countries’ energy infrastructure.
The crown prince during Saturday’s call sought clarity from Trump on what potential new action he was considering taking against Iran, the person said.
A White House official confirmed that the leaders spoke on Saturday.
Saudi Arabia earlier this week joined the US in striking multiple logistics and weapons sites used by Iranian-backed militias in Iraq, but has been urging the US and Iran to get back to the negotiating table to find an endgame to the five-month-old conflict.
The crown prince also dispatched his brother, Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman, to Washington earlier this week for separate meetings with Trump and Vice President JD Vance to discuss Iran strategy.
The stakes for continued US military action are high for Trump and his party as the conflict, unpopular among many Americans, has jolted the world economy just months before critical midterm elections in November.
The president had vowed to take retaliatory action after the US military thwarted a surprise attack earlier this week by Iran on a US base in Jordan.
He told reporters on Friday that “we just want to win” in Iran and said the US will hit Iran “very hard” until they can’t take it anymore.
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt expressed frustration that Tehran had last month signed a memorandum of understanding with the US on a truce but then quickly “broke it, shot at commercial ships, and killed American soldiers”.
On Saturday, the US State Department issued new security alerts for Americans in 10 countries in the region to exercise heightened caution due to the escalating tensions with Iran.
The warnings – covering Bahrain, Israel, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and United Arab Emirates – urged US citizens to prepare for the possibility of flight cancellations, temporary airspace closures and other travel disruptions.

Trump says US-Israeli attacks on Iran cancelled as ‘perimeters of a deal’ reached
The new deal ‘would include the immediate, complete and total’ opening of the Strait of Hormuz, claimed the United States president.
United States President Donald Trump said on Sunday that his country’s military and Israeli forces will halt attacks on Iran as “the perimeters of a deal” had been agreed upon.
The new deal “would include the immediate, complete and total” opening of the Strait of Hormuz and an end to “Iran’s nuclear threat”, Trump said in a social media post.
This comes more than five months after the conflict in West Asia began on February 28. Since then, two peace talks held between Washington and Tehran have collapsed.
The first round of talks that were held in Pakistan’s Islamabad collapsed on April 12, but the ceasefire in the region had largely held for nearly two months.
On June 15, the US and Iran arrived at an interim agreement to stop the fighting and reopen the strait for commercial vessels. They also held talks in Switzerland aimed at reaching a final peace deal within two months.
However, on July 8, Trump said that the ceasefire was “over”.
As a consequence, the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterbody connecting the Gulf to the Arabian Sea, remains effectively blocked for most international commercial vessels, triggering a global energy crisis. About 20% of global petroleum supply passes through the maritime chokepoint.
On Sunday, Trump claimed that he had been asked by Iran and other countries in West Asia “to hold off any attack in that the perimeters of a deal has been agreed to”.
The US president said that he has agreed to “cancel the attack”, subject to Tehran and Washington “rapidly making a deal”, for the “survival of a successful and prosperous Iran”.
He also said that Israel had agreed to work with the US to finalise the peace agreement with Iran.
Iran is yet to comment on Trump’s announcement.
The US and Israel had launched an attack on Iran on February 28, claiming that Tehran’s action posed an existential threat to Israel. Iran retaliated by striking Israel and US military bases in the region, targeting major cities in Gulf countries and ships.
Israel has been claiming that Iran is close to obtaining a nuclear weapon, which could alter the regional security balance. Tehran has long maintained that its nuclear programme is for civilian purposes.

Conditions For A Deal With Tehran
While the cancellation of the strike signals a temporary reprieve from total escalation, Trump emphasised that the pause is entirely conditional on Iran's readiness to 'rapidly make a deal'.
'The USA is locked and loaded and ready to go against the Islamic Republic of Iran, at levels of Military Terror, Strength, and Power not seen since World War II. The account emerges against a backdrop of mounting concerns about the depletion of advanced US interceptor missiles after months of military activity in the Middle East.
While the fresh agreement announced by US, with no official confirmation or acceptance from Iran, offers a temporary reprieve from total escalation, the cessation of the conflict is entirely conditional on the swift finalisation of the text.

U.S. President Donald Trump said on Saturday that he had canceled a planned attack on Iran after Tehran had agreed in principle to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and negotiate an end to its nuclear program.
In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump said the U.S. military was “locked and loaded” and prepared to launch an attack against the Islamic Republic with force “not seen since World War II.”
Trump said Iran and other regional countries had asked Washington to hold off because “the perimeters of a deal” had been agreed. He said the proposed terms would include the “immediate, complete, and total” reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and “an end to Iran’s nuclear threat.
“Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the world and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a deal,” the president wrote.
Israel “joins me in this commitment,” Trump said in the post, adding, “Get to work, everybody, and get it done.”
The American military and the Israel Defense Forces had been planning to restart joint attacks on Iran, targeting critical energy infrastructure sites, possibly beginning this weekend, CBS News reported on Saturday, citing unnamed U.S. officials.
Asked on Friday about talks to end the conflict with the Islamic Republic, Trump had said that Iranian negotiators were making him “angry.”
“I’m losing faith in them because they do lie and do, they do misrepresent,” he said.
Moshe Passal, a legislator for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s ruling Likud Party, told JNS on Sunday that as long as the Islamic regime remains in power in Iran, it will continue to pose a significant threat to the world.
“As long as confronting the problem is postponed, the price we pay will only grow. When the world faced Hitler, there were those who said, ‘Let’s reach an agreement,’” Passal said.
“In the end, there was no choice—the world had to defeat him, and that came at a cost. People in Britain, the United States, Europe and around the world paid the price. I don’t believe any agreement can be reached with this regime.”
Meanwhile, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that Iran is now willing to reach an agreement over denuclearization since it no longer has its “conventional shield” of drones and missiles to hide behind.
Speaking on Saturday night with Fox News’ Lara Trump, the daughter-in-law of the president, Rubio said that “I don’t think the Iranian regime has ever faced a president like President Trump, which is someone that actually takes action.”
Tehran still has drones and missiles, which can inflict damage, but degrading its military capabilities has allowed the U.S. to approach the Iranian regime “from a position of strength, not from a position of weakness,” the secretary of state said.
Likud Party Knesset member Amit Halevi told JNS on Sunday that the Iranian regime poses the greatest threat to the free world and would ultimately have to be defeated militarily.
“I think that in the last century, had the West not taken the initiative, Washington would still be locked in a major struggle against Hitler, Japan and others today. We are facing a barbaric, totalitarian and racist enemy, and we need to treat it accordingly,” Halevi said.
“I am sure that sooner or later President Trump—and whoever occupies the White House after him—will have to enter this battle, because it’s here, and it’s not going anywhere,” he added.
Brig. Gen. (res.) Amir Avivi, founder and chairman of the Israel Defense and Security Forum, told JNS on Sunday that while Trump appears willing to allow more time for diplomacy, he is unlikely to give Iran much of it.
“We have to remember that the attack may have been postponed, but Iran remains under a full blockade, so in a sense, the war is still ongoing. The big question is how long the president will be willing to negotiate and whether the Iranians are serious,” Avivi said.
He argued that the United States and Israel can cripple the Iranian regime by depriving it of its economic assets and its ability to sustain itself through a short military campaign.
“I don’t believe the Iranians are going to agree to anything, and I don’t think these talks will achieve anything on the nuclear issue. Ultimately, they are only postponing what is inevitable: striking the regime hard and bringing it to its knees,” he said.

sources.news_title: Planned US, Israeli strike on Iran suspended amid hopes of diplomatic breakthrough
sources.text:
World News
Planned US, Israeli strike on Iran suspended amid hopes of diplomatic breakthrough – Trump
President Donald Trump says the United States has suspended plans for a major military strike against Iran after receiving assurances that negotiations toward a broader agreement are close to completion.
In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump said the US military was fully prepared to launch an attack against the Islamic Republic but decided to hold off following requests from Iran and several Middle Eastern countries seeking more time for diplomacy.
According to Trump, the proposed agreement would include the immediate and complete reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and measures aimed at eliminating what he described as Iran’s nuclear threat.
He said the decision to suspend military action was made in the interest of global stability and to allow negotiators an opportunity to finalise the deal.
Trump also stated that Israel had agreed to support the decision to delay any large-scale military action while diplomatic efforts continue.
“The United States is ready if necessary, but we are giving peace a chance,” Trump said, expressing hope that negotiators would swiftly conclude an agreement.
Since tensions with Iran escalated, Trump has repeatedly warned of possible military action against Iranian targets, while also pausing such plans on several occasions after indicating that mediators had reported progress toward a negotiated settlement.

sources.news_title: Fresh uncertainty surrounds Iran war talks after Trump calls off strikes
sources.text:
Here's the latest
• Strikes called off: US President Donald Trump said he is canceling a planned attack on Iran, contingent on the two sides “rapidly” making a deal. He touted progress in talks, including on reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian state media gave no indication that Tehran asked for the attacks to be called off or has changed its stance on the vital waterway.
• Diplomatic efforts: Trump’s move came after Saudi Arabian state media reported Prince Mohammed bin Salman pushed for deescalation. No strikes were reported from either the Iranian or US side overnight into Sunday, following the announcement.
• Economic impact: The collapse of the initial US-Iran ceasefire last month has been followed by greater disruptions to global shipping and oil production, and Americans are facing high gas prices as a result. In Iran, economic problems are mounting after months of conflict.
Catch up on Iran talks, oil production and more of Sunday's top headlines
If you’re just joining us, we’ve been covering the uncertainty surrounding the state of Iran war talks, as well as the conflict’s persistent economic impacts.
We’re awaiting the open of the oil futures market at 6 p.m. ET, which will provide our first glimpse at prices since US President Donald Trump said this weekend that he was holding off on new strikes against Iran for now.
Trump said he is canceling a planned attack on Iran, contingent on the two sides “rapidly” making a deal. He touted progress in talks, including on reopening the Strait of Hormuz. But Iranian state media gave no indication that Tehran asked for the attacks to be called off or has changed its stance on the vital waterway.
The collapse of the initial US-Iran ceasefire last month has been followed by greater disruptions to global shipping in the strait and elsewhere in the region, and Americans are facing high gas prices as a result.
Here’s what else is happening:
- The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its allies, known as OPEC+, has agreed to increase oil production in September in light of the disruptions to the energy market.
- Iran’s understanding with Oman on a new shipping route does not mean the Strait of Hormuz will reopen, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei told Iran’s Islamic Republic News Agency. There have been ongoing negotiations between the countries regarding management of the strait.
- Iranian media outlets have reacted with glee and mockery to Trump’s announcement about holding off on strikes. Iranian state media claimed the US president was retreating, not responding to diplomatic developments.
- Meanwhile, Iranian officials have acknowledged mounting domestic economic and social problems after five months of the conflict. Iran’s unemployment has worsened since the conflict began, and its currency has hit new lows.
CNN’s Mohammed Tawfeeq, Auzinea Bacon, Tim Lister and Issy Lippolis, Andrew Carey, Abeer Salman and Ibrahim Dahman contributed to this report.
Iran-Oman understanding does not mean Strait of Hormuz will reopen, Tehran says
Iran’s understanding with Oman on a new shipping route does not mean the Strait of Hormuz will reopen, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei told Iran’s Islamic Republic News Agency (IRNA).
There have been ongoing bilateral negotiations between Iran and Oman regarding a mutual mechanism to manage the strait.
“The understanding between Iran and Oman regarding a new route is unrelated to the reopening or continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz,” Baqaei said, describing the agreement as “a necessary condition, but not a sufficient one.”
Baqaei blamed the strait’s closure on “the United States’ breach of commitments, the US naval blockade of Iran,” and added, “therefore, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz is an entirely different equation.”
OPEC+ agrees to increase September production
The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its allies, known as OPEC+, has agreed to increase oil production in September as the Strait of Hormuz remains impassable to maritime traffic.
The oil-producing group will raise daily output by another 188,000 barrels a day, marking the cartel’s sixth consecutive agreement to increase production amid the war with Iran. The increase completes the commitment to gradually unwind a 2023 decision to cut production by 1.65 million barrels a day.
The big picture: The group’s statement did not mention the war with Iran or disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz, through which about 20 million barrels of oil transited before the war began. Ship traffic through the strait has declined in recent weeks due to renewed strikes between the US and Iran. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has also targeted ships attempting to transit the strait.
In a video conference, OPEC’s Joint Ministerial Monitoring Committee “expressed concern regarding attacks on energy infrastructure,” which will increase market volatility and require costly and time-consuming repairs.
Oil market disruptions have also been exacerbated by the Russia-Ukraine conflict and Iran-backed Houthi rebels effectively blocking the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, through which Saudi oil flows. That waterway provided an alternate route from the Strait of Hormuz.
Oil prices have climbed and Americans have faced higher gas prices since the initial US-Iran ceasefire agreement collapsed last month.
Here's your US gas prices update for Sunday
We continue to track the Iran war’s impact on oil and gas prices, which have been rising since renewed fighting in the Middle East once again impacted shipping in the region.
The oil futures market opens at 6 p.m. ET, providing our first glimpse at prices since US President Donald Trump said this weekend that he was holding off on new strikes against Iran for now.
How the US-Iran ceasefire originally broke down last month
As we’ve been reporting, President Donald Trump says the US is canceling a planned attack on Iran subject to a deal being reached “rapidly,” citing progress in talks.
The last major diplomatic breakthrough came in June, when the two sides signed a memorandum of understanding about pausing fighting while they negotiated a lasting end to the war. This broke down following clashes centered on the Strait of Hormuz, resulting in the resumption of the US blockade and a renewed, expanded regional conflict.
Here’s a look back at how fighting originally resumed:
- July 1: US and Iranian negotiators travel to Doha, Qatar, for indirect negotiations. The delegations make “positive progress,” Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari says.
- July 7: Iran fires on three commercial vessels in Oman’s territorial waters near the Strait of Hormuz, according to a US official. US Central Command says it launched strikes against Iran as “punishment.”
- July 8: Iran warns it will deliver a “crushing response” to the US strikes, and the country’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it has launched attacks at 85 US military targets across Bahrain and Kuwait. Trump castigates Iran as “evil, sick people” at the NATO summit in Turkey, saying the memorandum of understanding “is over.” Hours later, the US launches more strikes against Iran.
- July 9: Tehran says the US military has struck a railway bridge in northern Iran. CENTCOM says the US has hit around 90 military targets in another round of strikes. A US official tells CNN that both countries are continuing to engage in technical negotiations on nuclear issues.
- July 10: Trump says the US has agreed to continue talks with Iran, but also that Washington has informed Tehran the ceasefire is no longer in effect. Iran’s chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf says Tehran is prepared for “all-out defense” if the US breaks the agreement. The Trump administration imposes fresh sanctions on Tehran.
- July 11: Iran’s foreign minister accuses the US of violating a clause on Tehran’s nuclear program in their agreement.
- July 12: The IRGC announces it has closed the Strait of Hormuz after firing a warning shot at a vessel attempting to use an unauthorized route to cross the waterway. The US military launches more strikes on Iran, and insists that the strait is still open.
- July 13: US attacks across Iran continue into the afternoon, killing at least two people, Iranian media reports. Trump says he will reinstate a blockade of Iranian ships in the Strait of Hormuz, and the US carries out more strikes on Iran overnight.
CNN’s Mohammed Tawfeeq, Hira Humayan, Pamela Brown, Lex Harvey, Zachery Cohen, Jessie Yeung, Kevin Liptak, David Winkie, Isaac Yee, Clay Voytek, Betsy Klein, Aida Karimi, Lauren Kent, Jennifer Hansler, Rhea Mogul, Dalia Abdelwahab, Aleena Fayaz, Izzy Lippolis, Aileen Graef and Piper Hudspeth Blackburn contributed to this post.
Iran not shifting on claim to supervise Strait of Hormuz
“Trump the fool has run out of steam!”… “Trump once again backed away from his hollow threats.”
Those were some of the rhetorical jibes in Iranian media outlets on Sunday, after US President Donald Trump claimed the foundations had been laid for a deal with Tehran – subject to a swift mechanism to open the Strait of Hormuz for all shipping.
The US president again insisted Iran must relinquish its hold on the channel. However, Iranian news agencies gave no indication that Tehran’s position had changed. Iran has repeatedly sought to control maritime traffic in the waterway — through which ships carried about one fifth of the world’s oil supply before the war.
Technically, both Iran and Oman have Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZ) in the Strait. But that does not allow them to impede shipping.
According to the United Nations, a state has “sovereign rights” to explore, exploit, conserve and manage the natural resources of the waters in its EEZ.
However, under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), “ships of all States, whether coastal or land-locked, enjoy the right of innocent passage through the territorial sea.”
A coastal state should not “hamper the innocent passage of foreign ships through the territorial sea,” it says, except in specific outlined scenarios. It may “take the necessary steps in its territorial sea to prevent passage which is not innocent,” UNCLOS outlines.
CNN’s Tim Lister and Sana Noor Haq contributed reporting.
Palestinians say White House is pressing Israel to halt Gaza strikes
US President Donald Trump’s Truth Social post overnight made clear to Israel there will be no immediate strikes on Iran, instead pointing to another round of talks to reach a lasting agreement.
And it’s not just Iran where the US is actively pursuing diplomacy.
Trump has also re-invested efforts to bring about progress in Gaza — and that means putting pressure on Israel to halt its attacks there.
The Palestinian enclave remains subject to ongoing Israeli strikes, despite Trump announcing a breakthrough three days ago. In one of the latest attacks, a family of three were killed in a strike near Gaza City overnight, a Palestinian hospital director told CNN.
Hamas has said it is committed to disarmament, as Trump announced last week, but only if Israel ceases fire, among other conditions.
“The coming hours will be a test of seriousness, not intentions,” a senior Hamas official told CNN on Saturday evening.
Mohammed Dahlan, a one-time Palestinian Authority leader in Gaza, now effectively exiled in the United Arab Emirates, wrote on Facebook that Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, was “working with the Israeli side to halt the attacks on Gaza.”
Dahlan’s wider influence is contested but he is seen as having remained close to various US administrations over many years.
CNN has reached out to the White House and State Department for comment.
While Netanyahu has not spoken publicly about Gaza developments since Trump’s announcement of Hamas’s promise to disarm, Israel’s Energy Minister, Eli Cohen, said there was no deal to halt attacks on Gaza and that he saw a need for Israel, which already controls 70% of the Strip, to take full control of it, in comments reported by Reuters.
What to know about the Strait of Hormuz
A crucial bargaining chip throughout the US and Israel’s war with Iran has been that of the Strait of Hormuz - a vital waterway that been effectively closed by Tehran since the fighting began in late February.
On Saturday, US President Donald Trump insisted the “perimeters of a deal” to halt strikes and immediately reopen the Strait “has been agreed to” after Iran and other regional countries urged the White House to “hold off any attack.” Iranian media swiftly rebuffed those claims, instead saying Trump had retreated.
As Tehran and Washington issue mixed messages, the status of the Strait remains at the core of the conflict. The narrow waterway passing between Iran and Oman serves as the main route for shipping crude from oil-rich countries such as Saudi Arabia, Iraq and Kuwait to the rest of the world.
Iran controls the strait’s northern side. About 20 million barrels of oil, or about one-fifth of daily global production, used to flow through the strait every day, according to the US Energy Information Administration, which calls the channel a “critical oil chokepoint.” According to the EIA, “very few alternative options exist to move oil out of the strait if it is closed.”
The strait also carries about one-fifth of global trade in liquefied natural gas.
Energy analysts have warned that oil and natural gas prices are likely to remain elevated until the strait is passable, even as Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates seek to expand other routes to get their crude to market.
Iranian state media denies Tehran asked Trump to call off strikes — here's the latest
Iran has given no indication it asked President Donald Trump to call off planned strikes on the country, after Trump said he had cancelled the attacks, citing a progress in talks.
The US president said he agreed to requests by Iran and other Middle Eastern countries “to hold off any attack in that the perimeters of a deal has been agreed to.”
Here are the latest developments:
- Iranian denial: Iranian media outlets have reacted with glee and mockery after Trump’s announcement. Iranian state media gave no indication that Iran had asked for the attacks to be called off, instead claiming Trump had retreated.
- Phone call: Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman held a phone call with Trump in which he pushed for a deescalation of tensions in the Middle East, Saudi Arabia’s state news agency reported. Earlier, sources told CNN that the crown prince raised concerns over plans to strike Iran during the call.
- No strikes: No strikes were reported from either the Iranian or US side overnight into Sunday, following the announcement from Trump. Strikes in the region have been relatively calmer over the past few days.
- Mounting woes: While persistently defiant in the face of US threats, Iranian officials have acknowledged mounting economic and social problems after five months of conflict. Iran’s unemployment has worsened since the conflict began, and its currency has hit new lows.
CNN’s Tim Lister and Issy Lippolis contributed to this post.
Trump’s Iran announcement presents a fresh challenge for Netanyahu
In announcing he was calling off strikes on Iran, US President Donald Trump said “Israel joins me in this commitment.”
But Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is yet to comment — and that’s probably not surprising.
Netanyahu was in the Oval Office as recently as Tuesday and might have hoped he had convinced the fickle US president of Israel’s arguments on both Iran and Gaza. But the start of the working week in Israel finds its leader grappling with setbacks in both areas.
Netanyahu is desperate for the US to resume its military campaign against Iran in earnest.
Convincing Washington to launch a major war was a triumph for the Israeli leader. But from Netanyahu’s perspective, and that of much of the Israeli public, it ended prematurely.
Israel is less concerned about energy prices and the freedom of shipping companies to move oil out of the Persian Gulf. In Israel, it’s Iran’s nuclear program and the regime behind it that matters.
They both look secure, and that makes Netanyahu vulnerable as the country moves to a general election in under three months’ time.
On Gaza, Netanyahu’s office was already signalling concerns ahead of Trump’s declaration Thursday evening that Hamas had agreed to disarm, in what the US leader called a “monumental step towards lasting peace and security.”
Israel believes Washington is too quick to want a win and too ready to reach accommodations with Hamas to that end. Netanyahu wants no restrictions on Israel’s freedom to do what it wants in Gaza, and here, too, Israeli public opinion is largely behind him.
Netanyahu will be keen to delay, or indeed scuttle if he can, any US-led efforts to halt strikes on Gaza or make any significant withdrawals, even if any pullbacks are to positions still well inside the enclave.
Defiant toward Trump, Iran faces growing woes at home
While persistently defiant in the face of US threats, Iranian officials have acknowledged mounting economic and social problems after five months of conflict.
“Today’s war is not just a war of missiles,” President Masoud Pezeshkian said last month, speaking at a meeting of Iran’s Supreme Judicial Council.
“The most important battlefield today is the economy and livelihood of the people. If economic pressures cause social discontent to form and this discontent spreads, the enormous social capital that the people have created in support of the system will be lost.”
Iran’s unemployment has worsened since the conflict began, and its currency has hit new lows. In June, the annual inflation rate stood at 88%, according to official data.
A US blockade of its ports, which was reinstated last month after a brief lull, as well as a resumption of US sanctions on its oil exports have strained already fragile public finances.
Add to that regular power cuts in the broiling summer heat and shortages of medicines such as insulin, as well as billions of dollars in damage to infrastructure: roads, railways, ports and industrial plants.
Neglect of problems in the south, which has borne the brunt of US attacks, means an opportunity has been lost “to prevent economic dissatisfaction from turning into a social divide. As a result, southern Iran has become the front line of a crisis,” reported the moderate media outlet Asriran on Sunday.
Iran’s public finances did benefit from the lull in the conflict that allowed it to resume exports. Between March and late July, Iran’s oil export revenue totalled $7.5 billion, according to the Iranian oil ministry -– compared to less than $5 billion in the same period last year.
But the overall picture is gloomy. The International Monetary Fund has projected that Iran’s real GDP will shrink by 6.1% this year.
Saudi crown prince urged deescalation in call with Trump, state media reports
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman held a phone call with US President Donald Trump in which he pushed for a deescalation of tensions in the Middle East, Saudi Arabia’s state news agency reported on Sunday. Earlier, sources told CNN that the crown prince raised concerns over plans to strike Iran during the call.
CNN earlier reported that Trump spoke with Saudi Arabia’s crown prince on Saturday, according to four people familiar with the matter and a regional source. Multiple people familiar with the matter said the crown prince raised concerns about plans for potential strikes on Iran during the call.
Trump has since called off the strikes, citing a progress in talks.
Iranian media deny Tehran asked Trump to halt attacks and mock US president
Iranian media outlets have reacted with glee and mockery after US President Donald Trump’s announcement late Saturday that he will hold off further strikes against Iran.
“We have just been asked by Iran, and other Middle Eastern Countries, to hold off any attack in that the perimeters of a deal has been agreed to,” Trump said in a social media post. “This would include the Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT.”
Iranian state media gave no indication that Iran had asked for the attacks to be called off or that Tehran’s position on the Strait of Hormuz had changed. Iran has insisted on a role in managing traffic through the strait.
Instead, Iranian media claimed it was Trump who had retreated.
“Trump the fool has run out of steam!” posted the semi-official news agency Fars.
“The Americans’ mountain gave birth to a mouse once again,” said Morteza Semiari, a political commentator in Tehran, according to Fars, using a Persian proverb.
Trump had “backed away from his positions once again after about a week of boasting and threats against Iran, claiming that an agreement was close,” said KayhanOnline, which is directed by Iran’s Supreme Leader.
“Whether he continues his aggression or backs down, our forces remain at the highest level of readiness and have prepared for every possibility,” Mehr added in another post.
Several Iranian news agencies picked up recent reporting in western media, including CNN, about growing shortages of US air defense missiles, which was “one of the main factors behind Donald Trump’s decision to halt the attack on Iran,” said the semi-official Tasnim news.
No strikes reported overnight from US or Iran
No strikes were reported from either the Iranian or US side overnight into Sunday, following an announcement by President Donald Trump that he is calling off a planned attack on Iran, contingent on being able to make a deal.
Strikes in the region have been relatively calmer over the past few days, although Kuwait said Iran hit a building belonging to a Chinese company in the northern part of the country on Thursday, killing one employee. The country’s armed forces said they intercepted drone attacks on Saturday, and blamed `’Iranian aggression`’.
Trump announced Saturday night he was canceling the planned strikes after Iran and “other Middle Eastern countries” asked him to “hold off.”
How Iran’s proxies have proven their value in widening Middle East conflict
After three difficult years, armed groups loyal to Tehran appear to be bouncing back across the Middle East, reinforcing Iran’s leverage in its war with the US and Israel.
For decades, experts say, these groups played a key role: acting as a powerful deterrent against direct attacks on Iran. The “Axis of Resistance” – an anti-Israel and anti-Western alliance of regional militias backed by the Islamic Republic – was, however, significantly weakened by Israel’s large-scale military response to the 2023 Hamas attack and the regional repercussions that followed.
It was when this axis was in a weakened state that direct conflict between Israel, the US and Iran erupted. Today, however, several armed groups allied with Tehran are back to pressuring Iran’s foes by opening new fronts that complicate the war and threaten to choke the global economy.
While those allies are back serving Tehran’s interests, they are not without political motivations of their own.
“Iran’s relationship with these groups is more complex and multifaceted than the common media practice of referring to them as ‘proxies’ suggests,” Ali Ahmadi, a fellow at the Geneva Centre for Security Policy and Middle East Institute Switzerland, told CNN.
Gulf nations could suffer more if Trump went ahead with attack on Iran, analyst says
If US President Donald Trump pressed ahead with attacks on Iran, it would deal further blows to the Gulf nations already on the receiving end of Tehran’s counterattacks, a political analyst told CNN Sunday.
Trump announced he was canceling planned strikes on Iran late Saturday evening, citing progress in talks. Earlier, CNN reported that Trump held a call with Saudi Arabia’s Prince Mohammed bin Salman and the crown prince raised concerns about plans for potential strikes on Iran.
“I think the Saudis don’t have confidence that the US has a winning military strategy,” said Trita Parsi, executive vice president of Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft. “All that would lead to is more suffering for them without actually changing the facts on the ground or changing the direction of this conflict.”
“It’s all loss, no gain,” he said, adding that “they know that type of escalation will only lead to a counter-escalation by the Iranians in which they see GCC (Gulf Cooperation Council) states will be the biggest victims.”
Trump's latest pullback comes as US forces face increasing strains
Once again US President Donald Trump has pulled back from a threatened escalation of US strikes on Iran.
Trump said in a Truth Social post that the US military was “locked and loaded and ready” to unleash “levels of Military Terror, Strength, and Power not seen since World War II,” but decided to call off strikes as Tehran and other Middle Eastern countries asked to “hold off any attack.”
Analysts noted the economic pressure the war has put on US allies around the region as to why they’d like to see hostilities stop. And they noted Iran faces those same economic hardships as well as a military that has been severely degraded by over five months of war.
But it’s also a military that retains a punch, as demonstrated by deadly strikes on US forces in the region in the past month.
Meanwhile, the US military is facing some tough questions about its ability to defend US forces as stocks of Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors are becoming increasingly stretched.
A report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies last week found the US inventory of Patriot interceptors, the prime defensive missile in the American arsenal, was at about a third of its pre-war level, from 2,330 to between 759 and 827 as of July 27.
THAAD interceptors, designed to hit ballistic missiles well before they near their targets, are down from 452 before the war to 278 or fewer now, according to the CSIS report.
The expenditure of those munitions goes along with other losses of materiel, including fighter jets, airborne early warning and reconnaissance planes, helicopters and drones.
At sea, US naval assets have seen extended deployments, which can push back needed maintenance and repairs.
“For an expansive, modern, and highly capable military like the US joint force, readiness hits are cumulative, while trade-offs are immediate,” Ariane Tabatabai, senior fellow at the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, wrote in June.
Almost two months later, the US joint force has been stretched even further, leading to questions on whether it can deliver a knockout blow in the war.
Trita Parsi, co-founder and executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, said on CNN Sunday that Iran has been able to keep fighting back every time the US increases military pressure – and could probably do so again.
“The bottom line is: Trump does not have an escalatory way out of this conflict,” Parsi said.
CNN analyst: Saudis and Iran faced pressure to avoid escalation
Announcing the cancellation of the planned strikes on Iran, US President Donald Trump said Saturday that Iran and “other Middle Eastern countries” asked him to hold off.
Earlier in the day, sources told CNN that Trump spoke with the Saudi crown prince, who raised concerns about potential new US attacks.
CNN military analyst Cedric Leighton, a former US Air Force colonel, said both Riyadh and Tehran need to avoid an escalation of hostilities in the region.
The Saudis are under pressure to get the Strait of Hormuz, through which much of their oil and other exports flow, reopened, Leighton said. “They’re economically at risk here,” he said.
Leighton noted that the Saudis, as a key US ally in the Persian Gulf, carry significant sway with Trump.
Iran is also facing economic challenges from the closure of the strait, according to Leighton.
But the military pressure on Tehran – after more than five months of war – has been taking a toll, he said, and the Iranians could use some relief.
“If it’s true that … there was pressure from Iran, then I think the Iranians are probably buying some time,” he said.
“They are certainly under some degree of pressure economically as well as militarily. But I also know that they are ready to, in essence, survive as much as they can,” Leighton said.
Latest in the Middle East: Trump says he's canceling new Iran attack
US President Donald Trump said on Saturday he is canceling a planned attack on Iran, citing progress in talks.
His comments came as no strikes have been reported from the US inside Iran in several days. US officials previously said fresh strikes could take place as soon as this weekend.
Trump said he agreed to requests by Iran and other Middle Eastern countries that he hold off from further attacks, and that the pause remains contingent on “being able to rapidly make a DEAL.” Earlier, CNN reported that Saudi Arabia’s Prince Mohammed bin Salman held a call with the president and raised concerns about plans for potential strikes on Iran, according to multiple people familiar with the matter.
A look at the latest headlines:
- US diplomatic officials renewed their warnings to American citizens in the Middle East, saying they should exercise caution and vigilance amid heightened tensions in the region.
- Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned that the country would respond forcefully to any further American “aggression.” In calls with regional counterparts on Saturday, he said Iran would respond in kind to any “adventurous action” by the United States.
- Iran also warned Gulf states that host American military bases, with Major Gen. Ali Abdollahi threatening that nations cooperating with the US “will burn in the fires of war.”
- A teenager arrested in January during widespread anti-regime protests in Iran was executed Saturday, according to a US-based activist organization.
- Global oil and gas prices have been rising again following renewed tensions between the US and Iran. The average price of gas in the US was over $4 on Saturday.
- Israeli strikes on Gaza left a huge crater at a hospital, local authorities said, days after Trump announced that Hamas and Israel had agreed to advance a ceasefire plan. Israel said it targeted Hamas weapon storage facilities in strikes across the Palestinian enclave.
CNN’s Izzy Lippolis, Jennifer Hansler, Sophie Tanno, Max Saltman, Abeer Salman, Ibrahim Dahman, Brad Lendon, Aida Karimi, Kevin Liptak and Zachary Cohen contributed reporting.
Sources: Trump speaks with Saudi crown prince amid push for resolution to US-Iran war
President Donald Trump spoke with Saudi Arabia’s crown prince on Saturday, according to four people familiar with the matter and a regional source.
Prince Mohammed bin Salman reinforced Saudi Arabia’s desire for de-escalation during the call and raised concerns about plans for potential strikes on Iran, multiple people familiar with the matter said.
Officials from mediating nations, including Qatar and Pakistan, have been urgently working to stave off a new escalation in the conflict, fielding calls with officials from Iran and the United States, including Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff, according to three people familiar with the matter.
An immediate goal has been to work out an arrangement between Iran and Oman to allow commercial traffic to resume flowing through the Strait of Hormuz.
CNN previously reported that the US was planning fresh strikes on Iran as soon as this weekend, citing two officials familiar with the plans.
“We will be hitting them very hard,” Trump said at a Cabinet meeting Friday. “At some point, they’re going to say, ‘We just can’t take it anymore.’”
Earlier in the week, US and Saudi fighter aircraft struck multiple sites in Iraq after drones were launched from Iranian-backed militias there toward Saudi Arabia.

sources.news_title: Trump holds off on new strikes against Iran amid emerging 'deal'
sources.text:
Donald Trump holds off on strikes against Iran, after Saudi prince raises retaliation concerns
Sun 2 Aug 2026 at 2:32pm
, updated
Sun 2 Aug 2026 at 7:14pm
In short:
US President Donald Trump says he will order American forces to hold off on new strikes against Iran, subject to a deal being reached.
Iran's Acting Defence Minister Majid Ibn al-Reza said his country would "neither be caught off guard nor remain passive", according to state media.
What's next?
Mr Trump says Middle East allies have reached the parameters of a deal, which would include a "total" opening of the Hormuz Strait and "an end to Iran's nuclear threat".
US President Donald Trump says he will order American forces to hold off on new strikes against Iran, saying Middle East allies have reached the parameters of a deal to end the five-month-old war.
The emerging deal "would include the Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT, and an end to Iran's nuclear threat," Mr Trump wrote on Truth Social.
"Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL."
Israel had agreed to join the US in the commitment to try to complete the agreement with Iran that would bring about an end to the war, he added.
Iran's Acting Defence Minister Majid Ibn al-Reza said Tehran viewed every threat from its adversaries as "real and credible", even if made as part of psychological warfare.
"We will neither be caught off guard nor remain passive," he said on Sunday according to state media.
Mr al-Reza said Iran would use threats as a basis to increase its military readiness, strengthen deterrence and enhance its military capabilities.
Saudis concerned about Iran retaliation
Before Mr Trump's announcement, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the kingdom's de facto leader, spoke with him by phone and raised concerns about the US potentially escalating the conflict with Iran, according to a person familiar with the leaders' discussion.
The Saudis, according to the person briefed on the substance of the call but not authorised to comment publicly, are concerned that Tehran could respond with attacks on the energy infrastructure of the kingdom and other Gulf countries.
The crown prince during Saturday's call sought clarity from Mr Trump on what potential new action he was considering to take against Iran, the source said.
A White House official, who was not authorised to comment publicly and requested anonymity, confirmed the leaders spoke on Saturday but did not offer any detail.
Kuwait said on Saturday it responded to a new round of drone attacks from Iran while a tanker was struck in the strategic waterway.
Israel carried out heavy strikes on the Gaza Strip after the Palestinian militant group Hamas agreed to disarm.
US threatened new strikes before announcement
Mr Trump on Friday had threatened more strikes on Iran as the US pressed for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
Speaking to reporters during a meeting with members of his cabinet at the Camp David presidential retreat in Maryland, Mr Trump said "we just want to win" in Iran and that the US would hit Iran "very hard" until it couldn't "take it anymore".
Later that day, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt expressed the US administration's frustration that Tehran had last month signed a memorandum of understanding on a truce but then quickly "broke it, shot at commercial ships, and killed American soldiers".
On Saturday, the US State Department issued new security alerts for Americans in 10 countries in the region to exercise heightened caution due to the escalating tensions with Iran.
The warnings, covering Bahrain, Israel, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, urged US citizens to prepare for the possibility of flight cancellations, temporary airspace closures and other travel disruptions.
New attacks on Kuwait and shipping
Kuwait's military said on Saturday that its forces were responding to drone attacks, which were part of Iran's assaults on the country.
In a statement, Major General Saud Abdulaziz Al-Otaibi, spokesperson for Kuwait's Defense Ministry, said the drones hit "a number of vital facilities", including a government structure in the country's north.
He said there were no casualties.
The British Navy said on Saturday that a tanker was struck and a separate explosion hit close to a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Oman.
No casualties were reported in either incident.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organisation said an unknown projectile hit the vessel on Friday, 11 nautical miles north-east of Lima, Oman.
The attack damaged the vessel's engine room.
The group said that on Saturday a large splash and an explosion were reported close to another tanker while it was sailing 21 nautical miles north-west of Khasab city.
Separately, crude oil appeared to be leaking and spreading in recent days from a sanctioned tanker grounded off the coast of Oman, close to a marine protected area, satellite images reviewed by the Associated Press show.
Iran has repeatedly attacked vessels attempting to transit through the Strait of Hormuz without its authorisation as part of its ongoing conflict with the US.
Israel strikes Gaza after Hamas says it will disarm
Intense Israeli strikes on Friday night and Saturday killed at least four people in central and northern Gaza and wounded dozens more, according to local health officials.
The strikes in Gaza followed evacuation warnings by Israel's military, which said on Saturday that it had struck Hamas targets across the territory and dismantled five Hamas storage facilities.
The strikes came after Hamas confirmed on Friday that it would disarm in a potential breakthrough for ending the war in Gaza, although major obstacles remain.
Palestinians in Gaza, most of whom are displaced or live in camps, received the news with both hope and scepticism.
A 24-year-old tuktuk driver, Abdel Moneim Aboul-Roos, who lost his leg in an Israeli strike, said he did not care about "talk about withdrawal and disarmament" as long as essentials such as food and medicine remained lacking.
Israel has not officially commented on the Hamas deal, which is part of a US-brokered ceasefire announced last October.
That agreement called for Hamas to disarm and hand over power to an independent Palestinian administration.
Israel was to withdraw and an International Stabilisation Force was to be deployed.
In a post on X, Israeli far-right lawmaker Itamar Ben-Gvir called the deal "unacceptable" and said the killings in Gaza must continue.
"Israel must win," he said.
Egypt, a key Gaza ceasefire mediator, lauded Hamas and other Palestinian groups for "their positive response" in the phased peace plan, Egyptian state-run media reported.

sources.news_title: Trump says he will hold off on new Iran attack in hope of quick deal
sources.text:
Trump says he will hold off on new Iran attack in hope of quick deal
CAIRO - President Donald Trump said late on Saturday, Aug. 1, he would hold off on a fresh attack on Iran as long as a deal could be reached quickly to halt Iran's nuclear ambitions and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran and "other Middle Eastern Countries" asked for a time to complete a deal that would lead to "the Immediate, Complete and Total" reopening of the Strait and "an end to Iran's nuclear threat," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform. "Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL."
Israel "joins me in this commitment," Trump wrote. Israel did not immediately make a public statement on the issue.
Iran warned the United States this weekend against any “adventurous action” and said it would retaliate decisively if American forces followed through on Trump's threats of fresh attacks on Iranian targets.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi’s comments in separate phone calls on Saturday with senior Turkish, Pakistani and Saudi officials came just hours after Kuwait's army said it destroyed hostile drones launched by Iran against several vital facilities.
Speaking to Pakistan's Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, Araqchi said Iran would respond decisively to any "aggression" and discussed the consequences of “destabilizing actions" by the U.S., as well as prospects for heightened regional insecurity, according to Araqchi's Telegram account.
Araqchi later told Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan that any attacks by the U.S. and Israel or participation by regional countries in such actions would be met with a “proportionate response.” Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman spoke to Trump on Saturday and "expressed concern and asked for clarity" about U.S. plans for Iran, a U.S. official told Axios.
The Saudi crown prince spoke to Trump, a White House official told Reuters, but did not provide details.
Nournews, a media outlet affiliated with Iran's top security body, said on Saturday that U.S. attacks on Iranian energy infrastructure would prompt Iranian strikes on oil fields in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, as well as the gas fields of Qatar and Israel, saying, "all will be burned to ashes."
At a cabinet meeting on July 31 at the Camp David retreat, Trump said he believed U.S. negotiators, including his son-in-law Jared Kushner, special envoy Steve Witkoff and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, could still reach a deal with Iran.
But Trump also said he was losing faith in the Iranians, saying, "They break their word so often" — a claim Tehran has frequently leveled at Washington — and said he would be "hitting them."
Strait of Hormuz incidents and oil prices
Oil prices have stayed high since U.S. and Israeli forces started the war with strikes on Iran on February 28. Trump has argued that his stated goal of keeping Iran from gaining nuclear weapons justifies higher fuel costs in the near term, but the economic pain has put political pressure on him to find a way to end the war.
Benchmark Brent crude futures rose 24% in July, and analysts polled by Reuters expect prices to rise further this year.
The risk of Iranian attacks has deterred most shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, an important conduit for global energy supplies, since the start of the conflict, sending shockwaves through the world economy.
A government facility in northern Kuwait and civilian property belonging to a company on Bubiyan Island were hit on Saturday, with falling shrapnel causing material damage but no casualties, the Kuwaiti army said.
Adding to the energy industry's concerns, Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen recently began threatening the Bab el-Mandeb, the strait at the other end of the Red Sea from the Suez Canal, another export route for Saudi crude.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said on Saturday it had received reports of two maritime incidents off Oman, including one in which a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile that damaged the engine room. In the other incident, the master of a tanker reported seeing a large splash and an explosion close to the vessel, though no damage was reported.
(Reporting by Yasmine Ghania and Menna Alaa El-Din in Cairo, Steve Holland in Washington DC; Writing by Matt Spetalnick; Editing by Sergio Non, Rod Nickel, Mark Porter and Kate Mayberry)

Washington, DC [US], August 2 (ANI): US President Donald Trump has announced the cancellation of a planned attack on Iran, subject to being able to rapidly make a deal with the Persian Gulf country, while noting that Israel has joined him in this commitment.
Trump said there have been urgent appeals from Middle Eastern Countries to hold off any attack as "perimeters of a deal has been agreed to". He asserted this would include immediate and total opening of the Hormuz Strait and an end to Iran's nuclear threat.
The announcement hinges on two pivotal concessions from Tehran: the unhindered opening of the Strait of Hormuz to re-establish international maritime traffic through the critical global energy chokepoint, and an enforceable end to Iran's nuclear advancement programme.
While the cancellation of the strike signals a temporary reprieve from total escalation, Trump emphasised that the pause is entirely conditional on Iran's readiness to " rapidly make a deal."
"The USA is locked and loaded and ready to go against the Islamic Republic of Iran, at levels of Military Terror, Strength, and Power not seen since World War II. Despite this, we have just been asked by Iran, and other Middle Eastern Countries, to hold off any attack in that the perimeters of a deal has been agreed to. This would include the Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT, and an end to Iran's nuclear threat," Trump said in a post on Truth Social.
"Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL. The Country of Israel joins me in this commitment," he added.
"Get to work, everybody, and get it DONE," Trump urged stakeholders, leaving the ball in the court of negotiators to translate the framework into a binding treaty.
Hours before Trump's announcement, Iran cautioned the United States against any "adventurous action", declaring that it would respond decisively should American forces launch fresh strikes on Iranian targets, thereby heightening tensions across the Middle East.
The warning followed remarks by US President Donald Trump on Friday, in which he said he was losing faith in talks with Tehran and threatened additional attacks, stating the US would be "hitting them" if required.
According to Araghchi's Telegram account, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi informed the Pakistani and Turkish officials that Iran would respond decisively to any "aggression" and reviewed the implications of what he termed destabilising moves by the US, along with the rising threat of regional instability.
Notably, the inclusion of Israel marks a significant diplomatic pivot as a top American military commander stationed in Europe also cautioned the Pentagon on Saturday that Washington may soon confront hard decisions on missile defence resources as the ongoing conflict with Iran continues to place heavy pressure on American military stockpiles.
The development was reported by The Washington Post, which noted that the chief of US European Command, Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, informed Pentagon officials earlier this week that the United States lacks adequate naval assets to continue intercepting Iranian ballistic missile strikes on Israel.
The account emerges against a backdrop of mounting concerns about the depletion of advanced US interceptor missiles after months of military activity in the Middle East.
While the fresh agreement announced by US, with no official confirmation or acceptance from Iran, offers a temporary reprieve from total escalation, the cessation of the conflict is entirely conditional on the swift finalisation of the text. (ANI)

Given Iran’s record of violating previously signed agreements, the president also noted that the United States remains “locked and loaded and ready to go against the Islamic Republic of Iran, at levels of Military Terror, Strength, and Power not seen since World War II.”
Trump said that for the attack to be canceled, Iran would need to show that it is abiding by the parameters of the deal, which include the immediate and complete opening of the Strait of Hormuz to international maritime traffic and an “end to Iran’s nuclear threat.”
He said that Israel has also agreed not to attack.
“The United States signed [a memorandum of understanding] with Iran and they broke it, shot at commercial ships, and killed American soldiers,” White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt previously told The Epoch Times by email. “President Trump is not going to stand by and allow this terrorist behavior to occur. Iran will continue to pay until they come to the table in, what President Trump deems, a meaningful way.”
Iranian Threats
Iranian officials earlier on Aug. 1 threatened new retaliatory attacks, including on U.S. allies in the region, if the United States were to act.
“We explicitly declare that Muslim countries must exercise foresight, monitor America’s crimes, and reconsider cooperation and alignment with the United States,” Iranian Maj. Gen. Ali Abdollahi said in a statement carried by the state-run Press TV on Aug. 1.

Iranian state media reported that Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi relayed similar warning messages in calls with Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan and Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan on Aug. 1.
Washington and Tehran reached a ceasefire agreement on April 8, and agreed to a memorandum of understanding for further peace negotiations in June. That ceasefire collapsed in July after Iranian forces renewed attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and its neighboring countries that have hosted U.S. military bases.
Following the renewed Iranian attacks, Trump ordered U.S. forces to launch new strikes on Iran. Those U.S. strikes continued for 13 days before pausing on July 25.
U.S. forces launched another set of strikes on Iran on July 29, in response to an attempted Iranian missile attack on a U.S. military outpost in Jordan. Kuwait’s military on Aug. 1 reported that its air defenses had intercepted multiple Iranian drones. Kuwait has hosted multiple U.S. military bases since the 1991 Gulf War.
On Aug. 1, the U.S. State Department issued a new travel advisory urging U.S. citizens in the Middle East to “consider departing” or be prepared to depart “should there be escalation.”
The warning was issued more than a week after at least eight U.S. embassies in the Middle East urged American travelers in the region to “exercise caution and heightened vigilance” and prepare for “flight cancellations, periodic airspace closures, and potential travel disruptions.”
The Aug. 1 update reiterates vigilance for Americans around the world, noting that “U.S. diplomatic facilities, including outside the Middle East, have been targeted” for attacks.
“Iran and groups supportive of Iran may target other U.S. interests overseas or at locations associated with the United States and Americans throughout the world, including U.S. businesses and other institutions,” the advisory reads.

sources.text:
WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump said Saturday that the United States and Israel had agreed to hold off on new strikes on Iran -- provided a deal to end the months-long conflict is "rapidly" reached.
Fears had mounted that the fighting could escalate once again after Trump threatened to hit Iran "very hard" and was reportedly considering renewed heavy attacks, including against energy infrastructure.
Trump said the US was "locked and loaded and ready to go against the Islamic Republic of Iran," but added that Tehran and other Middle Eastern countries had asked him to hold off on fresh strikes.
"Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL," Trump posted on his Truth Social platform.
The US president said the deal would have to include the "Immediate, Complete and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT, and an end to Iran's nuclear threat."
"The Country of Israel joins me in this commitment. Get to work, everybody, and get it DONE."
After more than five months of war, which began on February 28 when the United States and Israel launched strikes on Tehran, there is seemingly no end to the conflict in sight.
A previous ceasefire deal with similar terms, including the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, fell through, and Iran has since tightened its control over the vital waterway as the two countries resumed attacks against each other in recent weeks.
The resumption of hostilities has caused global oil prices, which had dipped during the initial ceasefire, to again rise.
And the back-and-forth comes just three months before midterm elections in the United States that could pose a challenge for Trump's Republican Party.
'Eager to do a deal'
US embassies in capitals across the Middle East had warned their citizens on Saturday to beware of "unforeseen escalation" in the regional conflict and urged them to be ready to leave.
CBS News said that the United States and Israel were planning joint strikes, possibly throughout the weekend, with oil refineries and power plants among possible targets.
But Trump said he ultimately decided to hold off on his threat of new attacks after requests from Gulf countries.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman called Trump on Saturday to express concerns about his strike plans, Axios reported, citing unnamed US officials.
One source with knowledge of the call told Axios that the Saudi crown prince had "urged Trump to de-escalate and refrain from launching the strikes".
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the report.
Iran and the US resumed exchanges of fire last month after a days-long lull in fighting, although there were no reported strikes overnight Friday to Saturday.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Fox News earlier in the week that the US had "wiped out" much of Iran's defenses, adding that Tehran was "now willing and in some cases seem eager to do a deal on denuclearization, to do a deal on the straits."
Still, he said Iran could "still do damage."
On Wednesday, a drone struck a US-owned gas vessel moored in an Egyptian port, causing a fire. Egypt is investigating but has not yet accused any group of launching the attack.
Meanwhile, an "unknown projectile" struck a tanker off the coast of Oman, a British maritime agency said on Saturday.
Iran has effectively maintained control over navigation through Hormuz since the outbreak of the war on February 28, requiring vessels to obtain permission and pay transit fees before using the waterway.
Maritime trade tracking firm Kpler said on Friday that traffic through the Hormuz strait has dropped "sharply".
On the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another waterway that has gained increasing importance as a transit route for Saudi Arabian oil, the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen on Saturday denied seeking to charge ships for passage through it.
The narrow waterway connects the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean and, via the Suez Canal, the Mediterranean.

The US's Gulf allies hold concerns that, while the American mainland is out of reach of Iranian missiles, countries like Bahrain, Jordan and the United Arab Emirates are not - with their critical infrastructure such as water desalination plans being prime targets.
