sources.news_title: Trump Halts Iran Strikes, Seeks Swift Diplomatic Agreement
sources.text:
Trump Halts Iran Strikes, Seeks Swift Diplomatic Agreement
After initially authorizing military strikes against Iran, Donald Trump abruptly halted the operation, signaling a shift towards diplomacy. The U.S. president now appears to favor negotiating a swift agreement over escalating military confrontation in the region.
TL;DR
- Trump postponed new strikes on Iran.
- Israel backed the decision to wait.
- Talks focus on the Hormuz Strait and nuclear deal.
Trump Halts Military Action, Pauses for Diplomacy
Amid heightened tensions in the Gulf, former U.S. President Donald Trump revealed that he chose to suspend planned military strikes against Iran. This decision, which received support from key ally Israel, has shifted attention back to high-stakes diplomatic negotiations involving the critical Hormuz Strait and the future of Iran’s nuclear program.
A Strategic Pause Backed by Israel
The move to delay further military escalation came after intense consultations with senior officials from both Washington and Jerusalem. According to sources close to the discussions, this pause was not made lightly. Several factors explain this decision:
- The potential risk of spiraling conflict in the Persian Gulf;
- Israel’s cautious stance favoring negotiation over immediate action;
- The ongoing efforts to secure commitments around Iran’s nuclear ambitions and regional shipping lanes.
The Hormuz Strait: A Global Flashpoint
At the heart of these deliberations lies the strategically vital Hormuz Strait, through which a substantial portion of the world’s oil supply transits. Recent incidents in these waters had reignited fears of a wider confrontation, prompting renewed calls for dialogue. Both American and Israeli officials now appear keen to explore avenues for reducing tensions while safeguarding their respective interests.
Nuclear Talks Remain Unresolved
Meanwhile, negotiations concerning Iran’s nuclear activities continue without a definitive breakthrough. Western officials remain wary of Tehran’s intentions, while Iranian leaders insist on their right to civilian nuclear technology. With major powers still divided over how best to contain potential threats, patience appears to be wearing thin—yet hopes persist that compromise might yet prevail.
As diplomatic efforts intensify, observers note that restraint by Washington—encouraged by Jerusalem—may offer a brief window for productive engagement. Whether this moment leads to lasting stability in the region remains uncertain, but for now, escalation has been set aside in favor of dialogue over force.

sources.news_title: Strait of Hormuz: ‘No new deal’ – Iran rubbishes Trump’s claim - NewsTmes.com.ng
sources.text:
Strait of Hormuz: ‘No new deal’ – Iran rubbishes Trump’s claim
Iran on Sunday denied that it entered a new agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
This is in direct contradiction to United States President Donald Trump’s recent claims. Trump had, while saying he has canceled a planned strike, announced that the outlines of a deal had been reached.
But Iran Fars news agency refuted the claim.
“There is no agreement on reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
“As long as the United States continues its hostile actions, the strait will remain closed,” the agency quoted a senior Iranian military source as saying.
The military source added that ships would be permitted to pass only through a designated route and with authorization from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy.
DAILY POST reports that the statement marked another sharp clash between Trump’s public account of negotiations and Iran’s version of events.
Recall that Trump early Sunday made the announcement that he had called off a planned American attack after Iran and several other Middle Eastern countries asked the US to refrain from striking, stressing that the basic parameters of a possible agreement had been settled.
“The US is locked and loaded and ready to go against the Islamic Republic of Iran, at levels of Military Terror, Strength, and Power not seen since World War II,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

sources.news_title: Trump Agrees to Pause Iran Strikes After Allies Report Deal Framework
sources.text:
President Donald Trump announced Saturday evening he would suspend new military strikes against Iran, saying Middle Eastern allies had reached the broad outline of an agreement to end the five-month-old war. Trump posted the announcement on Truth Social, stating the emerging framework would require the full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and a complete end to Iran's nuclear program.
Israel confirmed it would join the United States in working toward the agreement, according to Trump. The announcement came hours after Trump had told reporters at Camp David that the U.S. would strike Iran very hard until the country could no longer endure the pressure.
Saudi Arabia Presses for Restraint
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called Trump on Saturday and raised direct concerns about further U.S. escalation, according to a person familiar with the conversation reported by 6abc. Riyadh feared that strikes on Iranian energy infrastructure could provoke retaliatory attacks on Gulf states' own oil facilities.
The crown prince asked Trump for specifics on what military actions he was considering. A White House official confirmed the two leaders spoke but declined to detail the substance of the exchange.
Saudi Arabia had joined U.S. forces earlier in the week in hitting logistics and weapons sites linked to Iranian-backed militias in Iraq. Still, the kingdom has simultaneously pushed for a return to negotiations.
Diplomacy Around the Conflict
Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman traveled to Washington on Wednesday, meeting separately with Trump and Vice President JD Vance to discuss Iran strategy. Trump also hosted Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the White House on Tuesday — their first in-person meeting since the war began in February — where Netanyahu reportedly urged continued military prosecution of the conflict.
The war has weighed on the U.S. economy and carries political stakes ahead of November's midterm elections, according to reporting by the Associated Press via ClickOrlando.
Iran Signals It Will Not Stand Down
Iran's Acting Defence Minister Majid Ibn al-Reza said Tehran treats every threat from adversaries as credible, even those framed as psychological pressure. He said Iran would respond by building military readiness and strengthening deterrence, according to ABC Australia. He made clear the country would not be caught off guard.
Kuwait reported intercepting a new round of Iranian drone attacks on Saturday. A tanker was also struck in the Strait of Hormuz waterway during the same period.
State Department Warns Americans in Region
The U.S. State Department issued security alerts covering ten countries in the Middle East, urging American citizens to exercise heightened caution. The warnings applied to residents and travelers in Jordan, Israel, Iraq, Bahrain, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates.
Officials warned of potential flight cancellations, temporary airspace closures, and other travel disruptions tied to the escalating tensions.
Trump has announced pauses to strikes on Iran multiple times since the conflict began, according to ClickOrlando. Whether this latest halt holds depends on whether a formal deal can be concluded quickly, Trump said.

sources.news_title: Trump says US will delay new Iran attack while seeking quick deal – Axadle
sources.text:
President Donald Trump says the United States will postpone a new attack on Iran if Tehran can quickly agree to curb its nuclear programme and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
In a post on Truth Social last night, Mr Trump said Iran and other Middle Eastern nations had requested more time to reach an agreement that would bring about “the Immediate, Complete and Total” reopening of the strategic waterway and “an end to Iran’s nuclear threat”.
He did not identify the countries involved. The post came after a telephone conversation with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman of Saudi Arabia, a US ally.
“Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL,” Mr Trump wrote.
Iranian state media rejected the president’s account, saying Tehran had not asked Washington to halt its strikes. It described the claim as a “new lie” and said Iran’s armed forces remained fully prepared.
Iran says it is boosting deterrence
Mr Trump’s apparent step back, following days of threats from both sides, marked the latest turn in the conflict that the US and Israel launched five months ago.
The fighting has extended from the Gulf to the Red Sea and as far as a Mediterranean facility in Egypt.
Iran has largely shut the Strait of Hormuz, through which 20% of the world’s oil and LNG passed before the war. The disruption has driven energy prices higher and added to inflationary pressure worldwide.
Eli Cohen, Israel’s energy minister and a member of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s security cabinet, said Israel and the US remained in close security and intelligence coordination over developments across the region.
But he warned: “With or without an agreement, and regardless of any external commitments, if Iran attempts to renew its nuclear programme or advance its ballistic missile industries, we will be there. We will take action, and we will strike.”
Mr Trump and Mr Netanyahu met in Washington on Tuesday. An Israeli official said the discussions covered every possible route to restricting Iran’s nuclear programme, including diplomacy, economic pressure and military force. Tehran denies that it is pursuing a nuclear weapon.
Iran’s acting defence minister, Brigadier General Majid Ebn Al-Reza, said Tehran regarded recent US threats as “psychological and cognitive warfare” but was taking them seriously. Iran, he added, would strengthen its preparedness and deterrence rather than be caught unprepared or stand by passively, Press TV reported.
During his call with Mr Trump, the Saudi crown prince highlighted the “necessity of prioritising dialogue to de-escalate tensions” in the Middle East, Saudi Arabia’s state news agency said.
A White House official confirmed to Reuters that the conversation had taken place but offered no further details.
The risk of Iranian attacks has deterred most shipping through the Strait of Hormuz
Oil price surged last month
Speaking at a cabinet meeting on Friday, Mr Trump said he believed US negotiators — including his son-in-law Jared Kushner, special envoy Steve Witkoff and Secretary of State Marco Rubio — were capable of securing an agreement with Iran.
When an April ceasefire collapsed last month, benchmark Brent crude futures LCOc1 rose 24%. Analysts surveyed by Reuters expect prices to climb further this year.
Mr Trump has maintained that preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons warrants higher fuel costs in the short term. But the economic impact has intensified political pressure on his administration to find a route to ending the conflict.
Energy-sector concerns have also grown after Iran’s Houthi allies in Yemen began threatening the Bab el-Mandeb in recent days. The strait lies at the opposite end of the Red Sea from the Suez Canal and serves as another route for Saudi crude exports.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said it had received reports of two maritime incidents off Oman.
In one incident, an unidentified projectile hit a tanker and damaged its engine room. In the second, a tanker’s master reported seeing a large splash followed by an explosion near the vessel, although no damage was recorded.

Trump Halts Strike on Iran as High-Stakes Diplomacy Seeks to Avert Regional Conflagration
By: Fern Sidman
In a dramatic and potentially consequential recalibration of American foreign policy, President Donald Trump announced on Saturday that the United States has agreed to suspend a planned military strike on Iran, contingent upon the successful negotiation of a comprehensive agreement addressing both Tehran’s nuclear ambitions and the broader architecture of regional security. The declaration, delivered amid mounting geopolitical tension and intense diplomatic maneuvering, signals a precarious but notable shift toward de-escalation—one that hinges upon fragile negotiations and the strategic calculations of multiple global actors.
At the center of this unfolding diplomatic tableau lies a convergence of interests, anxieties, and geopolitical imperatives. According to individuals familiar with high-level discussions, the decision to pause the anticipated strike follows direct engagement between President Trump and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, whose intervention appears to have underscored the profound risks inherent in a further military escalation.
During a phone call described by sources briefed on the exchange, the Saudi leader expressed acute concern regarding the potential consequences of a U.S. attack on Iranian infrastructure. Specifically, the crown prince warned that targeting Iran’s energy facilities—or launching broader strikes against key strategic assets—could provoke retaliatory action against the oil infrastructure of Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states. Such a scenario, he implied, would not merely destabilize the region but could trigger cascading disruptions across global energy markets.
The crown prince’s message, as conveyed through these accounts, was unmistakably urgent. He sought clarity from President Trump on “what potential new action he’s weighing to take against Iran,” reflecting a deep apprehension within Riyadh that the conflict could rapidly expand beyond its current contours. The implicit warning was that even a limited strike might ignite a wider conflagration, drawing in multiple actors and jeopardizing the delicate balance of power in the Middle East.
President Trump, in outlining the rationale for the suspension, framed the decision not as a retreat but as a strategic recalibration designed to create space for diplomacy. He emphasized that the halt in military action is conditional, predicated upon Iran’s willingness to engage constructively in negotiations aimed at addressing what he described as “Iran’s nuclear threat” and ensuring the stability of critical regional corridors.
Among the most significant elements of the proposed framework is the full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, a maritime chokepoint through which a substantial proportion of the world’s oil supply transits. Trump indicated that the prospective agreement would guarantee unimpeded navigation through the strait, thereby alleviating one of the most persistent sources of global economic vulnerability.
“The proposed deal includes the full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz,” Trump stated, linking this objective to a broader effort to neutralize Iran’s capacity to threaten international shipping lanes. He further asserted that the agreement would entail an end to “Iran’s nuclear threat,” a formulation that encapsulates longstanding American concerns regarding Tehran’s enrichment activities and potential weaponization.
In a development that underscores the coordinated nature of the initiative, Trump also revealed that Israel has aligned itself with the diplomatic effort. By stating that Israel has “joined the commitment,” the president signaled a degree of consensus between Washington and Jerusalem that could prove pivotal in shaping the trajectory of negotiations. This alignment reflects a shared strategic interest in curbing Iran’s regional influence while avoiding an escalation that could imperil both nations’ security.
Nevertheless, the announcement represents a conditional de-escalation rather than a definitive resolution. The suspension of the strike is explicitly tied to the progress of negotiations, and the possibility of renewed military action remains firmly on the table should diplomatic efforts falter. In this sense, the current moment is best understood as an interlude—a pause in hostilities that affords negotiators a narrow window in which to pursue a durable settlement.
Crucially, Iranian authorities have not yet issued any formal confirmation that they accept the conditions outlined by Washington. The absence of an official response from Tehran injects a considerable degree of uncertainty into the process, raising questions about whether the proposed framework can secure the necessary buy-in from all parties involved. Analysts caution that without reciprocal commitments from Iran, the diplomatic initiative may struggle to gain traction.
The strategic significance of the Strait of Hormuz cannot be overstated. As one of the world’s most vital maritime arteries, the strait serves as a conduit for a substantial share of global oil exports. Any disruption to its operation has immediate and far-reaching implications for energy markets, international trade, and economic stability.
Consequently, the prospect of an agreement that ensures its uninterrupted functioning has been met with cautious optimism among market participants and policymakers alike.
Yet this optimism is tempered by an acute awareness of the complexities inherent in Middle Eastern diplomacy. The region’s intricate web of alliances, rivalries, and historical grievances renders any attempt at comprehensive agreement exceedingly challenging. The current initiative must navigate not only the bilateral dynamics between the United States and Iran but also the broader constellation of regional actors whose interests may not always align.
From a strategic perspective, President Trump’s decision to suspend the strike reflects a recognition of these complexities. By opting to pursue a negotiated solution, he has signaled a willingness to explore alternatives to military confrontation, even as he maintains the credible threat of force as leverage. This dual approach—combining diplomatic engagement with the implicit possibility of coercive action—has long been a hallmark of American foreign policy in the region.
At the same time, the involvement of Saudi Arabia introduces an additional layer of nuance. As a key ally of the United States and a principal rival of Iran, the kingdom’s perspective carries considerable weight. The crown prince’s intervention underscores the extent to which regional stakeholders are invested in avoiding a scenario that could spiral into a broader conflict with unpredictable consequences.
For global observers, the coming days will be critical in determining whether this diplomatic opening can be translated into tangible progress. Analysts emphasize that the success of the initiative will depend on the ability of negotiators to bridge significant gaps in trust, perception, and strategic priorities. The stakes are exceptionally high, with the potential outcomes ranging from a historic agreement that reshapes regional security to a breakdown in talks that reignites the specter of military confrontation.
The broader geopolitical context further complicates the picture. Tensions between Washington and Tehran have been characterized by cycles of escalation and de-escalation, often influenced by developments on the ground as well as shifts in domestic and international political dynamics. In this environment, even a seemingly minor incident can have outsized repercussions, underscoring the fragility of the current pause.
For now, however, the suspension of the planned strike represents a moment of cautious reprieve. It offers a glimpse of a possible path forward—one in which diplomacy, rather than force, serves as the primary instrument of conflict resolution. Whether this path can be sustained remains an open question, contingent upon the actions and decisions of leaders in Washington, Tehran, Riyadh, and beyond.
As President Trump himself has made clear, the pause is conditional and reversible. The United States stands ready to act should negotiations fail to produce the desired outcomes. In the meantime, the world watches closely, acutely aware that the choices made in the days ahead will reverberate far beyond the confines of the Middle East, shaping the contours of global security for years to come.

This decision aligns with recent discussions aimed at securing a ceasefire, where Trump emphasized the need for a rapid resolution to de-escalate hostilities. The situation remains fluid, with ongoing diplomatic efforts to address the underlying issues between the U.S. and Iran.

sources.text:
President Trump announced Sunday that the United States has agreed to hold off on a planned military strike against Iran after Iranian officials and Middle Eastern countries requested time to finalize the framework of a deal, sources confirmed. The proposed agreement would include the immediate reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and an end to Iran’s nuclear threat, with Israel supporting the decision to pause military action while negotiations continue.
“The strike has been canceled for now,” Trump indicated, making clear the reprieve is contingent on a deal being reached quickly. The announcement marks another dramatic reversal in a conflict that has seesawed between bombardment and diplomacy, coming just hours after Iranian state media denied any agreement to reopen Hormuz and insisted the waterway would remain restricted under IRGC control.
The pause follows intense speculation about imminent joint U.S.-Israeli strikes against Iranian energy infrastructure, including power plants and refineries, which sources said were being planned for the weekend. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had stated the Pentagon was “locked and loaded,” and Trump warned at a Camp David cabinet meeting that “we’ll be hitting them very hard” until Tehran capitulated.
Iran’s recent actions had appeared to close diplomatic windows. Tehran formally withdrew from the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, rejected an Omani proposal for joint Hormuz management, and launched an “attempted surprise” ballistic missile attack on a U.S. base in Jordan — the first such strike since Trump halted 13 consecutive nights of bombardment to pursue talks. All missiles were intercepted, but the escalation raised fears of a point of no return.
Trump’s decision to grant additional time suggests either confidence that Iranian negotiators are genuinely close to an acceptable framework, or recognition that weekend energy strikes would devastate global markets before financial exchanges opened Monday. The president had previously told Axios that diplomacy had “not much time” and that failure would trigger a return to “very strong military action.”
Whether this pause produces the comprehensive agreement Trump has demanded — including Hormuz reopening, uranium disposal, and verified nuclear constraints — or merely delays the inevitable resumption of hostilities depends on Iranian willingness to compromise on sovereignty claims and American tolerance for further provocations without retaliation.
Trump Pauses Planned Iran Strike for Talks
Trump agreed to hold off on planned military strikes against Iran after Tehran and Middle Eastern allies requested time to finalize a deal framework including immediate Hormuz reopening and ending Iran's nuclear threat, with Israel supporting the pause contingent on rapid progress.

sources.text:
The U.S. has agreed to pause attacks on Iran, President Donald Trump said Saturday, amid what he described as the “perimeters of a deal” being agreed upon, which would include the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
“We have just been asked by Iran, and other Middle Eastern Countries, to hold off any attack in that the perimeters of a deal has been agreed to,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social. “This would include the Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT, and an end to Iran’s nuclear threat.”
The president said the U.S. was “locked and loaded and ready to go” against Iran but that he agreed to cancel attacks “subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL.” He added that Israel, the U.S. partner in the war with Iran, “joins me in this commitment.”
“Get to work, everybody, and get it DONE,” Trump wrote regarding a possible new agreement.
The statement came after the State Department on Saturday urged Americans across the Middle East to consider leaving the region or be prepared to depart on short notice, warning of flight disruptions and security risks as the conflict appeared to be escalating.
Trump had earlier threatened Iran with additional attacks, saying Friday that the U.S. will be “hitting them very hard,” while Iran vowed to “punish” the U.S. as both nations traded heavy strikes.
“Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise caution and heightened vigilance and should be prepared for flight cancellations, periodic airspace closures, and potential travel disruptions,” the State Department said Saturday.
“Some airlines in the region have postponed resumption of earlier flight schedules; others have cancelled some routes. Americans in the region should consider departing, or be prepared to depart should there be escalation.” The State Department also urged Americans to reconsider travel to or through the region.
The warning was distributed through U.S. embassies in the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, and Saudi Arabia. The agency posted a nearly identical statement earlier this month, but that bulletin did not urge Americans to prepare to leave the Middle East or to reconsider upcoming trips, reflecting Washington’s growing concern that the conflict could widen.
On Saturday, the Kuwait Army said its air defense systems intercepted drone attacks from Iran.
“Kuwaiti air defenses are currently engaging hostile drone attacks following the Iranian aggression. The General Staff of the Army notes that any explosions heard are a result of air defense systems intercepting the hostile attacks,” the army stated.
Two days prior, the U.S. military confirmed it had executed a “heavy wave of strikes” on Iran, hours after reports surfaced that the president in a phone call had vowed to “beat the f—–g s— out of” the country.
A Trump ally stated that the president has grown increasingly exasperated with the state of the war, noting, “There was not a real strategy for how long or what they should do to get to the endpoint.”
The conflict has now entered its sixth month, despite early predictions that the war would resolve itself quickly. The protracted conflict has led to soaring global oil prices and rising gas prices in the U.S.
There was a brief reprieve from fighting in June when the U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding outlining the process for talks to end the war. However, in early July, Trump declared a ceasefire to be “over,” and the countries resumed striking targets across the Middle East.

New Delhi: US President Donald Trump on Saturday said he had cancelled a planned military attack on Iran after Tehran and other Middle Eastern countries asked Washington to hold back, claiming that the broad contours of an agreement had been reached.
Trump said the proposed arrangement would include the “immediate, complete and total” reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and an end to what he described as Iran’s nuclear threat.
However, he made clear that the suspension of military action was conditional on the parties quickly finalising a deal, leaving open the possibility of renewed strikes if negotiations failed.
“The U.S.A. is locked and loaded and ready to go against the Islamic Republic of Iran, at levels of Military Terror, Strength, and Power not seen since World War II,” Trump wrote on Truth Social in a post amplified by the White House.
“Despite this, we have just been asked by Iran, and other Middle Eastern Countries, to hold off any attack in that the perimeters of a deal has been agreed to,” he said.
Trump added that he had agreed to “cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL”.
He also claimed that Israel had joined the commitment to hold off military action and urged the parties to complete the negotiations.
There was no immediate public confirmation from the Iranian government that it had accepted the framework described by Trump. Israel had also not separately announced its agreement to the proposed terms at the time of publication.
What has Trump claimed?
Trump’s announcement contains three central assertions.
First, he said Iran and other regional governments had requested that the United States refrain from launching a planned attack.
Second, he claimed that the “perimeters”, apparently referring to the parameters or broad outlines, of a deal had been agreed.
Third, he said the emerging arrangement would fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz and eliminate the nuclear threat posed by Iran.
The statement did not explain how Iran’s nuclear programme would be restricted, dismantled or monitored. It also did not provide a timetable for reopening the waterway or identify the Middle Eastern countries involved in negotiating the framework.
Trump’s wording suggested that the understanding remained preliminary rather than a completed agreement.
Saudi Arabia pressed for restraint
The announcement followed diplomatic intervention by Saudi Arabia and other regional governments concerned that a large-scale American attack could trigger Iranian retaliation against Gulf energy infrastructure.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman raised concerns about a possible escalation during a telephone conversation with Trump on Saturday, according to a person familiar with the discussion.
Riyadh feared that strikes on Iranian energy facilities or other strategic targets could prompt Tehran to attack oil, gas and other infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and neighbouring Gulf countries.
The crown prince had also sent Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman to Washington for discussions with Trump and Vice-President JD Vance. Saudi Arabia has supported action against Iranian-backed groups but has simultaneously urged Washington and Tehran to return to negotiations.
Announcement follows fresh regional attacks
Trump’s decision came after another round of hostilities raised fears that the conflict could widen further.
Kuwait said on Saturday that its forces had responded to Iranian drone attacks on several vital facilities, including a government structure in the north of the country. No casualties were reported.
The British Navy also reported that a tanker had been struck near the Strait of Hormuz, while an explosion occurred close to another vessel travelling through the waterway.
An unknown projectile damaged the engine room of one tanker northeast of Lima, Oman, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations. A separate tanker reported a large splash and explosion northwest of Khasab.
The incidents followed American accusations that Iran had violated an earlier truce, attacked commercial vessels and killed US soldiers.
On Friday, Trump said the United States would hit Iran “very hard” until it could no longer continue fighting, while White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt warned that Tehran would “continue to pay” until it entered meaningful negotiations.

sources.news_title: Trump Agrees to Cancel Planned Strike on Iran, Conditional on Swift Agreement
sources.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump said the United States and Israel have agreed to suspend planned military strikes against Iran, following requests from Tehran and several countries in the region, stressing that the decision is contingent upon reaching an agreement within a short period.
In a post published early Sunday on his Truth Social platform, Trump said he had approved the cancellation of a planned attack on Iran after the parties agreed on what he described as the “broad outlines” of a potential deal.
Trump said the United States remains “fully prepared and ready to act” against Iran, with military capabilities “the world has not seen since World War II.”
He added that the request to postpone the attack came after agreement on a framework that includes the immediate, full, and complete reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the elimination of what he described as Iran’s nuclear threat.
Trump said he agreed to cancel the operation “for the good of the world and for the future prosperity and success of Iran,” while emphasizing that the cancellation remains conditional on the ability to finalize an agreement quickly.
He also said that Israel had joined the United States in supporting the temporary suspension of military action and called for negotiations to be concluded without delay.
Meanwhile, Iran warned against what it described as any “reckless action” by the United States, saying it would respond decisively if Washington carried out Trump’s threats of launching new attacks on Iranian targets.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi made the remarks during separate phone calls on Saturday with senior officials from Türkiye, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia, only hours after the Kuwaiti Armed Forces announced that they had intercepted and destroyed hostile drones launched by Iran toward several strategic facilities.
According to a statement posted on Araghchi’s Telegram channel, he told Pakistan’s Army Chief General Asim Munir and Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan that Iran would respond firmly to any aggression. He also discussed what he described as the destabilizing actions of the United States and warned of the potential for further regional instability.
Earlier on Saturday, the U.S. State Department urged American citizens in the Middle East to exercise heightened caution and prepare for the possibility of airspace closures, flight cancellations, and travel disruptions amid escalating regional tensions.
In a security advisory, the department advised U.S. citizens in the region to consider departing—or be prepared to do so if the situation deteriorates—and urged Americans elsewhere to carefully reconsider travel to or through the Middle East.
A White House official told Reuters that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had spoken with President Trump, but provided no further details about the conversation.
During a Cabinet meeting at Camp David on Friday, Trump said he believed U.S. negotiators—including Jared Kushner, Special Envoy Steve Witkoff, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio—could still reach an agreement with Iran.
At the same time, Trump said he was losing confidence in the Iranian leadership, stating that “they break their promises very often,” and warning that “I will strike them.”
Strait of Hormuz in Focus
Oil prices have remained elevated since U.S. and Israeli forces launched military operations against Iran on February 28.
Trump said his stated objective of preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons justified higher fuel costs in the short term, although the economic consequences have increased political pressure to bring the conflict to an end.
Brent crude futures rose 24% in July, and analysts surveyed by Reuters expect prices to climb further this year.
The risk of Iranian attacks has significantly disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important energy corridors, sending shockwaves through global markets.
On Saturday, the Kuwaiti military said a government facility in northern Kuwait and civilian property belonging to a company on Bubiyan Island were struck by falling debris, causing material damage but no casualties.
Adding to concerns over global energy supplies, Yemen’s Houthi movement, an Iranian ally, has recently threatened shipping through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, another strategic route for Saudi crude exports located at the southern entrance to the Red Sea.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) also reported two separate maritime incidents off the coast of Oman on Saturday. In one case, an oil tanker was hit by an unidentified projectile that damaged its engine room. In the second, the captain of another tanker reported seeing a large water plume and an explosion near the vessel, although no damage was reported.
Source: Reuters

sources.news_title: President Donald Trump Halts Planned Iran Attack After Deal Outline Agreed
sources.text:
President Donald Trump halts planned Iran attack after deal outline agreed
President Donald Trump canceled a planned U.S. military attack on Iran on Saturday, August 2, 2026, following requests from Tehran and other Middle Eastern countries. S. President Donald Trump announced on Saturday, August 2, 2026, that he had canceled a planned military attack on Iran. This decision came after Tehran and other Middle Eastern countries reportedly requested a halt to the strikes, citing an agreement on the “perimeters of a deal.” The unexpected diplomatic opening marks a potentially fragile shift in the ongoing conflict.
President Donald Trump communicated the development via his Truth Social platform, outlining that the proposed agreement would include the “Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT, and an end to Iran’s nuclear threat.” This came as U.S. media reports had suggested fresh strikes against Iran were imminent this weekend.
Diplomatic shift amidst heightened tensions
This sudden halt to military action follows weeks of escalating hostilities in a conflict that began on February 28, 2026. Hopes for a negotiated end to the war had dwindled, particularly after a temporary ceasefire, initiated by a memorandum of understanding on June 17, effectively broke down.
Before President Donald Trump’s announcement, U.S. Embassies in Iraq, Jordan, and the United Arab Emirates had issued urgent warnings. They advised American citizens in the region to exercise caution and prepare for potential flight cancellations.
Many were also told to consider leaving the region immediately. These warnings underscored the dire security situation, exacerbated by recent incidents like a tanker near Oman reportedly struck late Friday, with another vessel seeing an explosion nearby.
Iran’s Fars International state news agency, however, quickly dismissed President Donald Trump’s stated demands as merely a “wish list.” This immediate pushback from Tehran suggests the path to a comprehensive deal remains fraught with significant challenges and mutual distrust.
The terms of a tentative agreement
President Donald Trump articulated the core tenets of the potential agreement on Truth Social. He emphasized the necessity of an “Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT.” This critical global oil chokepoint historically saw approximately one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies pass through it before the war.
Beyond maritime access, the deal’s framework also targets “an end to Iran’s nuclear threat,” a long-standing point of contention for Washington and its allies. President Donald Trump also stated that “The Country of Israel joins me in this commitment,” indicating a coordinated diplomatic front with a key regional partner.
Despite the cancellation, President Donald Trump maintained a hardline stance. He warned that the U.S. remains “locked and loaded and ready to go” should diplomacy fail, highlighting the underlying military readiness that has characterized his administration’s approach.
Meanwhile, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi had previously warned against any “aggression” by the U.S. and Israel, or participation by regional countries. He stressed that such actions would be met with a “decisive and proportionate response,” according to Araqchi’s Telegram account.
Echoing this sentiment, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, cautioned that continued U.S. naval blockades and “warmongering” would not only tighten control over the Strait of Hormuz. He added that it would also “shut down other straits and chokepoints.” These warnings underscore Iran’s capacity and willingness to disrupt global shipping routes.
Broader conflict context and economic impact
The “war with Iran,” which commenced on February 28, 2026, with coordinated U.S.-Israeli airstrikes, has had devastating consequences. Codenamed “Operation Epic Fury,” the initial offensive aimed to dismantle Iran’s ballistic missile capabilities, eliminate its navy, and prevent nuclear weapon acquisition.
The conflict also sought to sever Iran’s support for proxy forces. President Donald Trump later claimed regime change had occurred, following the death of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in the initial waves of strikes.
The broader regional instability has had a clear impact on global markets, particularly energy prices. Rising energy prices illustrate the volatility sparked by escalating tensions across the Middle East.
On Friday, West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures rose over 1% to close at $84.67 per barrel. Brent crude, the international benchmark, also gained more than 1% to settle at $90.12. Prices had previously fallen more than 5% earlier in the week, fueled by fleeting hopes of de-escalation.
The war has been marked by retaliatory attacks. Iran targeted U.S. military bases in Kuwait and Bahrain following U.S. strikes against its Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targets. A drone strike on Thursday on two ships at Egypt’s Mediterranean port of Damietta also signaled the conflict’s expansion, though no one claimed responsibility.
A history of strained relations and pressure
The U.S. reimposed a naval blockade on Iranian ships on July 13, prohibiting their entry or exit from Iranian ports. This aggressive move followed previous waves of strikes that the U.S. had “completed” against Iran, hitting dozens of targets over the last week.
These actions are part of President Donald Trump’s long-standing “maximum pressure” campaign against Iran. The campaign has intensified dramatically during his current term, aiming to curb Iran’s regional influence and prevent its nuclear ambitions.
The role of key figures like John Ratcliffe, Director of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), who was pictured with President Donald Trump at Camp David on July 31, underscores the administration’s coordinated approach. Ratcliffe’s continued presence suggests the deep involvement of intelligence operations in the ongoing strategy.
The breakdown of the June 17 Memorandum of Understanding underscored the persistent gulf between the two nations on critical issues. Neither side has budged on key sticking points, including the future of Iran’s nuclear program and the control of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
This diplomatic setback earlier in the summer paved the way for renewed hostilities. It pushed the region closer to widespread military confrontation. Against this backdrop, President Donald Trump’s latest announcement represents a significant pivot, albeit one that remains highly conditional.
Implications for regional stability and global markets
The agreement on “perimeters of a deal” offers a narrow window for de-escalation, but its fragility is evident in Iran’s immediate dismissal of the terms as a “wish list.” The success of any rapid deal hinges on bridging these deep-seated differences, particularly concerning the nuclear program and maritime security.
Should a diplomatic resolution materialize, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz could alleviate some of the upward pressure on energy prices. This would provide a measure of stability to global markets, offering a potential reprieve for consumers and industries alike.
Conversely, a failure to secure a comprehensive deal could swiftly reignite military confrontations, with severe economic and human costs. The continued volatility highlights the high stakes involved for all parties.
The involvement of “other Middle Eastern Countries” in requesting the halt to attacks signals a broader regional desire for de-escalation. This collective plea could provide a crucial impetus for sustained diplomatic efforts, potentially fostering a more inclusive and durable peace process in the volatile region.
However, the underlying structural issues that fuel the conflict remain unresolved, including proxy warfare, competing regional hegemonies, and the enduring nuclear question. Any lasting peace will demand fundamental shifts in policy and perception from all parties involved, going beyond a temporary pause.
Broader geopolitical uncertainties, even beyond the direct conflict, can ripple through global economies, affecting various sectors. These broader market shifts underscore the interconnectedness of global finances, where stability in one region impacts all.
The global community will be watching closely as events unfold, with the specter of renewed conflict continuing to hang over the region. The interplay between diplomacy and military readiness will define the immediate future of U.S.-Iran relations and, by extension, the stability of the broader Middle East.
For now, the cancellation offers a temporary reprieve, preventing immediate bloodshed and allowing for a renewed focus on negotiations. But the path to a lasting solution remains exceptionally challenging, requiring delicate diplomacy and a genuine commitment to compromise from all sides.

Donald Trump announced late Saturday that he was calling off a fresh attack on Iran, provided a deal can be reached quickly to halt Iran’s nuclear program and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Iran and “other Middle Eastern Countries,” the president wrote on Truth Social, had asked for time to complete an agreement leading to the “Immediate, Complete and Total” reopening of the strait and “an end to Iran’s nuclear threat.” “Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL.” Israel, Trump added, “joins me in this commitment.” There was no immediate public statement from Jerusalem.
The announcement capped a day of crossed threats. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had warned Washington against any “adventurous action,” promising a decisive response. In phone calls with Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, Araghchi discussed the consequences of American “destabilizing actions.” He later told Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan that any U.S. or Israeli attack — and any participation by regional countries — would meet a “proportionate response.”
“Burned to ashes”
The starkest warning came from Nournews, an outlet affiliated with Iran’s top security body: if the United States strikes Iranian energy infrastructure, Iran will hit oil fields in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates and gas fields in Qatar and Israel. “All will be burned to ashes,” it said.
Gulf pressure was felt in Washington as well. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called Trump on Saturday and “expressed concern and asked for clarity” about American plans for Iran, a U.S. official told Axios. A White House official confirmed the call to Reuters without providing details.
The day’s attacks
Kuwait’s army said it destroyed hostile drones launched by Iran at several vital facilities. A government installation in the north of the country and civilian property belonging to a company on Bubiyan Island were hit by falling shrapnel, causing material damage but no casualties. The British-backed UKMTO reported two maritime incidents off Oman: a tanker struck by an unknown projectile that damaged its engine room, and a second vessel whose master reported seeing a large splash and an explosion nearby, with no damage.
Adding to the energy industry’s concerns, Iran’s Houthi allies in Yemen have begun threatening Bab el-Mandeb, the strait at the opposite end of the Red Sea from the Suez Canal and another export route for Saudi crude.
The economic pressure
Oil prices have remained high since the war began on February 28. Brent rose 24% in July alone, and analysts polled by Reuters expect further increases this year. The risk of Iranian attacks has deterred most shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, sending shockwaves through the global economy. Trump has argued that preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons justifies higher fuel costs in the near term, but the economic damage has translated into political pressure to end the war.
On Friday, at a Cabinet meeting at Camp David, the president said he still believed his negotiators — son-in-law Jared Kushner, special envoy Steve Witkoff and Secretary of State Marco Rubio — could reach a deal. But he also said he was losing faith in the Iranians, “They break their word so often” — the same accusation Tehran has long leveled at Washington — and announced he would be hitting them.

sources.news_title: When Trump’s Iran ‘deal’ isn’t a deal – it’s the third retreat in four months
sources.text:
COMMENTARY: By Lim Tean
Trump’s Iran “deal” isn’t a deal. It’s hos third retreat in four months.
April 2026: 48-hour ultimatum, then a two-week delay.
July: “13 straight days of strikes,” then a pause “to give peace talks some space.”
August 1: a fresh wave of attacks cancelled — the one he’d just threatened — citing “the perimeters of a deal”.
- READ MORE: Trump cancels planned attacks on Iran, calls for a deal to be made rapidly
- Other Lim Tean articles
The pattern never changes. Maximalist threat first, loud and absolute. Then an unsigned framework — no enforcement, no timeline, no verification.
Hormuz is still not open. Iran’s IRGC hit tankers under US “aerial escort” the Friday before this latest climbdown.
This is the Paper Shield exposed in real time. ABC’s own sourcing flags depleting Patriot interceptor stocks as a live constraint on further strikes.
Riyadh called Trump directly to caution against escalating. That’s not strength — that’s a president being managed by his own logistics tail.
Bluster works once. By cycle three, Tehran and Riyadh have both priced it in.
Iran will keep hitting tankers for exactly as long as it costs Washington nothing but words.
Malaysia stands firm
Meanwhile, Malaysia has just shown the world something rare — a government that won’t be bought.
An Israeli-American dual national was found at a tech retreat in Johor. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s answer was immediate: the dual nationality Israeli was asked to leave. Malaysia does not recognise Israel — full stop.
Washington’s response? The US summoned Malaysia’s ambassador. Eight members of Congress gave Kuala Lumpur 15 days to reverse course or lose military education funding.
Anwar’s answer: “That will not deter us.”
This is what I call the Legitimacy Principle in action — a government’s strength isn’t measured by how much force it can project, but by whether its people, and the wider world, believe it’s doing the right thing.
Anwar has just bet that standing firm on Palestine is worth more than Washington’s money.
Watch closely: this is the same logic that slowly made apartheid South Africa unsustainable — not one act, but the accumulation of states refusing to pay the price of complicity.
Small states rarely get to write the rules. Every so often, one gets to show what happens when it refuses to be governed by them.
Lim Tean is a Singaporean lawyer, politician and commentator. He is the founder of the political party People’s Voice and a co-founder of the political alliance People’s Alliance for Reform. He also hosts Lim’s Substack.

sources.news_title: Trump Halts Massive Iran Strike: Strait Of Hormuz To Open Under New Peace Deal
sources.text:
United States President Donald Trump has made a significant and startling announcement regarding the escalating tensions in the Middle East. In a move that has captured global attention, Trump stated that the United States won't proceed with a planned military strike against Iran, while this decision comes as a result of a draft agreement for a historic deal that could potentially avert a large-scale war. According to the President, the United States was fully prepared to launch a massive assault on the Islamic Republic of Iran, but the operation was halted at the last moment due to the progress made in diplomatic negotiations.
The Scale of the Planned Military Action
President Trump revealed that the United States had finalized all preparations for a forceful attack against Iran. He described the planned military action as being of a magnitude not seen since the Second World War. Writing on his platform, Truth Social, Trump emphasized that the US was ready to deploy military power and strength on a scale that would have been unprecedented in modern history. However, this massive strike was postponed following appeals from Iran and other nations in the Middle East. The President clarified that the decision to delay the military action was based on the condition that a comprehensive deal would be reached quickly.
Key Terms of the Proposed Peace Deal
The proposed agreement includes several critical conditions that Iran has reportedly agreed to follow. A primary component of the deal is the permanent opening of the Strait of Hormuz. This maritime route is considered one of the most vital passages for global trade and energy supplies, while in the past, Iran has frequently threatened to close the strait, causing significant concern in international markets. Under the new parameters, Iran has committed to keeping the Strait of Hormuz open at all times. On top of that, the deal stipulates that Iran will completely terminate its nuclear weapons program, ensuring that the country never develops a nuclear bomb. This move is seen as a major step toward eliminating the threat of nuclear conflict in the region.
Regional Cooperation and Israel's Involvement
President Trump highlighted that the path to this potential peace involved significant mediation and appeals from Middle Eastern allies. These countries requested the United States to delay military action as they had reached the parameters of a deal to end the 5 month long conflict. Trump noted that these regional partners are working toward a resolution that would bring stability to the area. Crucially, the President mentioned that Israel is also part of this agreement. Israel has agreed to work alongside the United States to move this commitment forward, signaling a unified front in the pursuit of regional peace. Trump urged all parties involved to continue their efforts to finalize the deal, stating that everyone should get to work to complete it.
Advisory for United States Citizens
Prior to the announcement of the deal, the United States had been in a state of high alert, and an advisory had been issued for American citizens in the Middle East. The advisory warned that several airlines might cancel their flights in the region in the coming days. There were also concerns regarding potential bombings and the possibility of American ambassadors being targeted by Iran, while consequently, US citizens were advised to consider leaving the Middle East or to be prepared for such an eventuality. This high level of preparation underscores how close the region was to a major military confrontation before the current diplomatic breakthrough.
A Vision for a Peaceful Future
In his communication, President Trump explained that his decision to choose the path of dialogue over military action was motivated by a desire for a safe and prosperous future for the world. He asserted that this move shouldn't be viewed as a sign of weakness but rather as a strategic decision for the benefit of global stability. Trump expressed his hope for a successful and happy Iran to continue to exist, provided the deal is finalized swiftly. He concluded by stating that the draft agreement represents a chance to end the threat of war and bring lasting peace to the Middle East, benefiting the entire world.

sources.news_title: Trump Delays Iran Strikes as Talks for Deal Continue - THE DESTINATION
sources.text:
Trump Delays Iran Strikes as Talks for Deal Continue
US President Trump Halts Planned Iran Strikes, Seeks Quick Deal to End Conflict
WASHINGTON: (News Desk) – President Donald Trump said Saturday that the United States and Israel have agreed to suspend plans for additional strikes on Iran, but only if a deal to end the ongoing conflict is reached quickly.
Tensions had risen after Trump warned that the US could launch major attacks against Iran, including possible strikes on energy facilities. He said Washington was prepared for military action but decided to delay further operations following requests from Iran and several Middle Eastern countries.
In a statement shared on his Truth Social platform, Trump said the pause would remain in place while efforts continued toward a potential agreement. He emphasized that any deal must include the immediate reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and guarantees to end concerns over Iran’s nuclear program.
Trump added that Israel had agreed to the same approach, urging negotiators to work toward a resolution.
The latest development comes after more than five months of conflict that began on February 28, when the US and Israel launched strikes on Tehran. Despite previous ceasefire efforts, fighting resumed in recent weeks, with both sides exchanging attacks.
The renewed tensions have affected global energy markets, pushing oil prices higher after earlier declines during a temporary ceasefire period. The situation also comes months before the US midterm elections, creating additional political pressure for the Trump administration.
Reports said US officials had been considering coordinated strikes with Israel, including possible attacks on Iranian oil facilities and power infrastructure. However, Trump said he backed away from those plans following appeals from Gulf countries, including Saudi Arabia.
The conflict has also raised security concerns across the Middle East. Several US embassies advised citizens to remain alert over possible escalation and prepare for potential travel disruptions.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Iran had suffered significant damage to its defenses and appeared more open to discussions on nuclear issues and the Strait of Hormuz, though he warned Tehran still had the ability to retaliate.
Meanwhile, maritime tensions continued, with reports of attacks on vessels in regional waters. A drone strike hit a US-owned gas vessel in an Egyptian port, while a maritime agency reported an unidentified projectile had struck a tanker near Oman.
The Strait of Hormuz remains a key global shipping route, and reduced traffic through the waterway has raised concerns about international oil supplies and trade.

August 02, World (LNW): US President Donald Trump has announced that planned American military strikes against Iran have been put on hold, saying the decision was made to allow space for a rapid diplomatic agreement aimed at easing tensions in the Middle East.

He indicated that any agreement would require Iran to eliminate what he described as its nuclear threat and ensure the immediate reopening of the strategically important Strait of Hormuz to international shipping.
Trump said the decision had been reached in consultation with Israel, despite reports in several US media outlets suggesting Washington had been preparing a major new wave of military action against Iranian targets over the weekend.
According to the US President, American forces were fully prepared to launch what he described as an overwhelming military operation against Iran. However, he claimed that appeals from Iran and several countries in the region to delay military action had prompted him to give diplomacy another opportunity. Trump also suggested that negotiators had already reached a broad understanding on the framework of a potential agreement.
Iran has yet to issue an official response to Trump’s latest remarks.
Earlier, Tehran accused Washington of further inflaming regional tensions, warning that any neighbouring country assisting the United States in military operations would face serious consequences.
Meanwhile, the US government has advised American citizens across the Middle East to remain vigilant amid the uncertain security situation. A security advisory warned travellers to prepare for possible flight cancellations, temporary airspace closures and wider travel disruptions should the conflict intensify.
Reports from US media, including CBS News, indicated that American and Israeli officials had been considering one of the most extensive bombing campaigns of the conflict, with energy infrastructure reportedly among the potential targets.
The proposals were said to have been discussed during a Cabinet meeting on Friday, where Trump reportedly warned that Iran would face severe military action if hostilities continued.
Separately, media reports claimed Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had spoken with Trump and expressed concern over the possibility of further military escalation, underscoring growing regional unease.
The confrontation between Washington and Tehran has intensified in recent months following the collapse of a ceasefire that had briefly halted fighting. Since then, both sides have exchanged a series of military strikes, while the United States and Israel have continued operations against Iranian targets.
Iran, in turn, has launched missile and drone attacks on US-linked assets in the region and has threatened maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for global energy supplies.
The prolonged conflict has continued to unsettle international markets, with renewed military tensions contributing to volatility in global oil prices and raising concerns over broader regional stability.

sources.text:

Trump decided to pause his planned attacks against Iran.
He is under pressure from Middle East countries against escalating.
Brent and WTI crude oil prices slipped sharply on Hyperliquid after President Donald Trump halted the planned attacks against Iran, citing requests from Iran and other Middle East countries. WTI dropped to $81, with its 24-hour volume hitting $181 million.
Brent, the global benchmark, dropped to $83, down sharply from last month’s high of $100. The two benchmarks remain substantially lower than where they were at the peak of the war.
Trump chickens out on planned attack against Iran
Brent and WTI oil prices tumbled after President Donald Trump decided against hitting Iran as most media organizations had predicted. CBS and the Wall Street Journal said that Trump had finally decided to bomb Iranian energy and other infrastructure projects. The attack was to start on Saturday and go on for a few weeks, with the goal being to pressure Iranians to reach a deal with the US.

Iran has dismissed President Trump's claims that negotiations are underway and making progress, insisting that no direct talks are taking place between Washington and Tehran. Iranian officials pointed to the latest U.S. strikes as evidence that diplomatic efforts have effectively broken down.
Those attacks ended the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) reached earlier, and they also marked the third time the Trump administration has launched military action against Iran during periods when negotiations were reportedly ongoing.

"The USA is locked and loaded and ready to go against the Islamic Republic of Iran, at levels of Military Terror, Strength, and Power not seen since World War II," Trump said late Saturday in a post on his Truth Social platform.
But the Trump administration said it would hold fire for now.
"Despite this, we have just been asked by Iran, and other Middle Eastern Countries, to hold off any attack," he said.
"Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL," he said.
The US president said the deal would have to include the "Immediate, Complete and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT, and an end to Iran's nuclear threat."
"The Country of Israel joins me in this commitment. Get to work, everybody, and get it DONE."
After more than five months of war, which began on February 28 when the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran, there is seemingly no end to the conflict, with a resumption of tit-for-tat attacks in recent weeks.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman called Trump on Saturday to express concerns about his strike plans, Axios reported, citing unnamed US officials.
One source with knowledge of the call told Axios that the Saudi crown prince had "urged Trump to de-escalate and refrain from launching the strikes."
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the report. (AFP)

sources.news_title: Trump announces deal parameters to end Iran war as US holds off on new strikes
sources.text:
Photo: Gage Skidmore from Surprise, AZ, United States of America / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0)
Trump announces deal parameters to end Iran war as US holds off on new strikes
The announcement triggered immediate market reactions, with Bitcoin and oil prices moving in lockstep as traders priced in the possibility of a ceasefire that Iran hasn't actually agreed to yet.
President Trump announced on June 12 that Mideast allies have established the parameters for a deal to end the Iran war, with the US agreeing to delay new military strikes while negotiations move forward.
What we know about the deal framework
The framework was facilitated by Pakistan, which has positioned itself as the primary mediator in the conflict. This builds on an earlier partial ceasefire that Pakistan helped broker back in April 2026, a temporary arrangement that slowed hostilities but never fully stopped them.
The next concrete milestone is the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, scheduled for signing on June 17. That document would establish a 60-day window for negotiating final peace terms.
Trump suggested on June 12 that the ceasefire agreement was close to finalization, with expectations that a signing event could take place in Europe shortly after the memorandum. The US decision to hold off on new strikes is clearly intended as a gesture of good faith to keep the diplomatic channel open.
But Iran has already pushed back on characterizations that a binding agreement exists.
The crypto angle is more real than you’d think
Iran began accepting Bitcoin for transit tolls in the Strait of Hormuz back in March 2026. The Islamabad Memorandum would reportedly pause those Bitcoin toll collections for 60 days during the negotiation window.
Bitcoin has shown notable correlation with oil price movements throughout this conflict. When the Strait of Hormuz is under threat, oil prices spike, risk sentiment deteriorates, and Bitcoin trades more like a risk asset than a safe haven. The pattern has been consistent enough that traders have started using oil futures as a leading indicator for short-term Bitcoin moves.
Why investors should stay cautious
The April partial ceasefire was supposed to be a stepping stone to peace, but by July, Trump declared the ceasefire “over” as tensions re-escalated, with Bitcoin trading between $61,000 and $63,000 during that volatile stretch. Markets initially rallied on ceasefire optimism, then gave back gains when the truce collapsed.
The 60-day negotiation window built into the Islamabad Memorandum creates a defined period of uncertainty, especially when one of the principal parties is already disputing whether any agreement actually exists. The Islamabad Memorandum signing on June 17 will be the next real data point, and even that only starts the clock on negotiations rather than ending the conflict.

sources.news_title: Trump says he will hold off on fresh Iran attack in hope of a quick deal on nuclear threat, Hormuz
sources.text:
Trump says he will hold off on fresh Iran attack in hope of a quick deal on nuclear threat, Hormuz
Middle Eastern nations have asked for time to complete an agreement leading to the strait’s reopening, he adds
[CAIRO] US President Donald Trump said late on Saturday (Aug 1) that the US would hold off on a fresh attack on Iran, as long as a deal could be reached quickly to halt Iran’s nuclear ambitions and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran and other Middle Eastern countries asked for time to complete a deal that would lead to “the immediate, complete and total” reopening of the vital strait and “an end to Iran’s nuclear threat”, Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform. The post followed a call with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman of Saudi Arabia, a US ally.
“Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the world and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a deal,” Trump wrote. Israel “joins me in this commitment”, he said.
Eli Cohen, Israel’s energy minister and a member of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s security Cabinet, said there was close security and intelligence coordination between Israel and the US on things happening in the region. But he added: “With or without an agreement, and regardless of any external commitments, if Iran attempts to renew its nuclear programme or advance its ballistic missile industries, we will be there. We will take action, and we will strike.”
Trump and Netanyahu met on Tuesday in Washington, with an Israeli official saying they had explored all possible paths to curb Iran’s nuclear programme, including diplomacy, economic pressure and force. Teheran denies seeking a nuclear weapon.
Press TV reported that Iran’s acting defence minister, Brigadier General Majid Ebn Al-Reza, said Teheran viewed recent US threats as “psychological and cognitive warfare” but was treating them seriously, adding that Iran would boost preparedness and deterrence rather than be caught off guard or remain passive.
In his call with Trump, the Saudi crown prince stressed the “necessity of prioritising dialogue to de-escalate tensions” in the Middle East, Saudi Arabia’s state news agency reported. A White House official said the two had spoken but did not provide details. Trump’s apparent de-escalation after days of threats of new attacks from each side marked the latest turn in the war that the US and Israel launched five months ago.
Attacks have spread across the Gulf to the Red Sea and even a Mediterranean facility in Egypt. Iran has largely closed the Strait of Hormuz, a conduit for 20 per cent of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas before the war, causing energy prices to stir and stoking broader inflation.
Iran’s semi-official Mehr news agency reported on Sunday that Iranian military officials had dismissed Trump’s claim that Teheran had sought to halt attacks as “a new lie” aimed at pressuring Gulf Arab states. They said Iran’s forces are on the highest level of readiness whether the US escalated or withdrew, warning that if confrontation became unavoidable, the battlefield would decide the outcome.
Teheran had earlier warned the US against any “adventurous action” and said it would retaliate decisively to any fresh attacks on Iranian targets.
Pressure on Trump grows as oil surges
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told senior Turkish and Pakistani officials in phone calls on Saturday that Teheran would respond decisively to any “aggression” and discussed the consequences of “destabilising actions” by the US, as well as prospects for heightened regional insecurity, he posted on the Telegram messaging platform. Hours earlier, Kuwait’s army said it had destroyed hostile drones launched by Iran against several vital facilities. Araghchi said he told Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan that any attacks by the US and Israel or participation by regional countries in such actions would be met with a “proportionate response”.
Agreement possible?
At a cabinet meeting on Friday, Trump said he believed US negotiators, including his son-in-law Jared Kushner, special envoy Steve Witkoff and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, could reach a deal with Iran.
As an April ceasefire in the war unravelled last month, benchmark Brent crude futures jumped 24 per cent, and analysts polled by Reuters expect prices to rise further this year.
Trump has argued that his stated goal of keeping Iran from gaining nuclear weapons justifies higher fuel costs in the near term, but the economic pain has put political pressure on him to find a way to end the war.
Adding to the energy industry’s concerns, Iran’s Houthi allies in Yemen in recent days began threatening the Bab el-Mandeb, the strait at the other end of the Red Sea from the Suez Canal, another export route for Saudi crude.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations said on Saturday that it had received reports of two maritime incidents off Oman.
In one, an unknown projectile struck a tanker, damaging the engine room. In the other, the master of a tanker reported seeing a large splash and an explosion close to the vessel, though no damage was reported. REUTERS

Iran warned the US this weekend against any “adventurous action” and said it would retaliate decisively if American forces followed through on Trump’s threats of fresh attacks on Iranian targets.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman spoke to Trump on Saturday and “expressed concern and asked for clarity” about US plans for Iran, a US official told Axios.
The Saudi crown prince spoke to Trump, a White House official told Reuters, but did not provide details.
Nournews, a media outlet affiliated with Iran’s top security body, said on Saturday that US attacks on Iranian energy infrastructure would prompt Iranian strikes on oil fields in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, as well as the gas fields of Qatar and Israel, saying, “all will be burned to ashes”.
At a cabinet meeting on Friday at the Camp David retreat, Trump said he believed US negotiators, including his son-in-law Jared Kushner, special envoy Steve Witkoff and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, could still reach a deal with Iran.

A government facility in northern Kuwait and civilian property belonging to a company on Bubiyan Island were hit on Saturday, with falling shrapnel causing material damage but no casualties, the Kuwaiti army said.
Adding to the energy industry’s concerns, Iran’s Houthi allies in Yemen recently began threatening the Bab el-Mandeb, the strait at the other end of the Red Sea from the Suez Canal, another export route for Saudi crude.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said on Saturday it had received reports of two maritime incidents off Oman, including one in which a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile that damaged the engine room.
